cohort.label: 2020–2024 Board of County Commissioners
cohort.transition_reason: Swearing-in of Durham County's historic first all-female Board on December 7, 2020 following the November 3, 2020 election. Newly elected commissioners Nida Allam and Nimasheena Burns joined returning incumbents Brenda A. Howerton, Wendy Jacobs, and Heidi Carter, succeeding retiring 32-year veteran Ellen W. Reckhow and outgoing Vice Chair James Hill. Annual Chair/Vice Chair rotation: Dec 7, 2020–Dec 3, 2023 Brenda A. Howerton (Chair) and Wendy Jacobs (Vice Chair); Dec 4, 2023–Dec 1, 2024 Nida Allam (Chair) and Nimasheena Burns (Vice Chair).

conflicts.issue: Approval vs. Continuance of $750,000 ARPA Award to Knox Street Studios (Item 24-0245)
conflicts.summary: The Board split 4-1 over whether to approve a $750,000 ARPA contract for Knox Street Studios immediately or defer it to the May 6 work session for further review, raising sharp tensions over equity and contract vetting standards.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the $750,000 Knox Street Studios contract immediately without further delay, while scheduling both Forward Cities and Knox Street Studios to present at the May 6 work session.
side_a_arguments: Staff under Economic Development Director Andy Miracle had vetted the allocation timeline since December 2023 and March 2024.
Forward Cities received $1.5 million in ARPA funds without being pulled or delayed, making additional holds on Black-led Knox Street Studios inequitable.
Scheduling both organizations for May 6 provides transparency without stalling contract execution ahead of federal ARPA deadlines.
conflicts.side_b_position: Continue item 24-0245 to the May 6 work session before voting so commissioners can examine contract terms and the 50/50 split between administrative staff and pass-through funding.
side_b_arguments: Commissioners should not vote on a $750,000 nonprofit contract without sufficient work-session briefing and clarity on deliverables.
Requests for review were driven by fiduciary diligence regarding contract structure rather than the race of the recipient.
conflicts.resolution: Howerton's continuance motion failed for lack of a second, and the main motion to approve item 24-0245 with May 6 presentations from both recipients passed 4-1.

conflicts.issue: Non-Renewal and Immediate Relief of County Manager Wendell Davis
conflicts.summary: The board split 3-2 over Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs's motions to not renew County Manager Wendell Davis's contract (terminating June 29, 2021) and to relieve him of his duties immediately.
conflicts.side_a_position: Exercise Section 4 of the County Manager's contract to not renew his agreement and relieve him of duties immediately pending an interim appointment.
side_a_arguments: Board has contractual authority under Section 4 to decide on non-renewal and comply with all contract obligations.
Board needed an immediate transition to an interim county manager.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose non-renewal and immediate removal as unwarranted, racially motivated, and procedurally unfair.
side_b_arguments: Decision was made without consulting Black board members and without completing a formal performance appraisal or board training.
Wendell Davis maintained seven straight years of strong county financial standing and school-building progress.
Action constituted retaliation for Davis and county staff raising racial bias concerns, while failing to implement Coleman Report and Racial Equity Task Force recommendations.
conflicts.resolution: Both motions passed 3-2 on roll-call votes (Ayes: Allam, Carter, Jacobs; Nays: Burns, Howerton).

conflicts.issue: Extension of Outside Attorney Denise Smith Klein's Contract Without Confirmed Total Cost
conflicts.summary: Commissioners split 3-2 over extending outside counsel Denise Smith Klein's contract to assist with executing the manager contract termination and related obligations.
conflicts.side_a_position: Extend Klein's existing contract at her existing hourly rate to assist with executing all obligations flowing from the board's decisions.
side_a_arguments: Acting County Attorney Willie Darby advised that extending an existing contract did not require a new RFP.
An existing hourly rate was already set in Klein's current engagement, making the motion sufficiently definite.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose extending the contract without a confirmed cost ceiling, RFP, or Klein's confirmation of rates for expanded scope.
side_b_arguments: Klein's prior contract covered only document review, whereas execution work could entail different costs.
Voting on a contract without a defined price or prior board discussion of cost violates sound fiscal stewardship and risks litigation.
conflicts.resolution: Motion passed 3-2 (Ayes: Allam, Carter, Jacobs; Nays: Burns, Howerton), with Acting Attorney Darby noting Klein could decline the extension terms.

conflicts.issue: Hiring Outside Attorney Denise Smith Klein to Review the County Manager's Contract
conflicts.summary: After closed session, commissioners split 3-2 on authorizing Acting County Attorney Willie Darby to finalize an engagement letter with outside attorney Denise Smith Klein to review the County Manager's contract.
conflicts.side_a_position: Retain outside counsel Denise Smith Klein to review the County Manager's contract and hold separate consultations with each commissioner.
side_a_arguments: Secures independent outside legal review and individual commissioner consultations regarding the County Manager's contract.
conflicts.side_b_position: Rely on in-house county attorneys for contract interpretation without spending extra taxpayer money.
side_b_arguments: County attorneys on staff are competent to interpret contracts as a normal function.
Using taxpayer funds for an outside attorney on a task staff can perform is wasteful and unfair.
conflicts.resolution: Motion carried 3-2 (Ayes: Allam, Carter, Jacobs; Nays: Burns, Howerton).

conflicts.issue: Motion to Compel Commissioner Heidi Carter's Recusal from the County Manager's Contract
conflicts.summary: Following closed session, Chair Brenda A. Howerton moved (seconded by Nimasheena Burns) to require Commissioner Heidi Carter to recuse herself from commenting on or participating in the County Manager's contract, which failed 2-3.
conflicts.side_a_position: Require Commissioner Carter to recuse herself from comments and involvement in the County Manager's contract based on precedent from prior meetings.
side_a_arguments: Precedent from prior meetings warranted Carter's recusal from discussions and decisions on the manager's contract.
conflicts.side_b_position: Reject forced recusal and allow Commissioner Carter to participate in deliberations on the County Manager's contract.
side_b_arguments: Commissioner Carter stated unequivocally that she would not recuse herself regardless of the vote.
Commissioner Nida Allam cited legal advice/communications previously received by the board in voting no.
conflicts.resolution: Motion failed 2-3 on roll call; Commissioner Carter remained seated on the matter.

conflicts.issue: Selection of BOCC Vice Chair (Nimasheena Burns Nomination vs. Wendy Jacobs Election)
conflicts.summary: The newly seated board divided 2-3 against Chair Brenda A. Howerton's nomination of Nimasheena Burns for Vice Chair and then elected Wendy Jacobs 3-2.
conflicts.side_a_position: Elect newly seated Commissioner Nimasheena Burns as Vice Chair to reflect racial equity and community advocacy for Black and brown women's leadership.
side_a_arguments: Chair Howerton cited extensive community emails and racial equity considerations in nominating Burns.
conflicts.side_b_position: Reject Burns's nomination and elect veteran Commissioner Wendy Jacobs as Vice Chair.
side_b_arguments: Heidi Carter, Nida Allam, and Wendy Jacobs voted No on Burns's nomination; Allam and Jacobs are recorded voting Aye on the 3-2 ballot electing Jacobs (with Howerton voting Nay and Carter/Burns split in the unrecorded gap).
conflicts.resolution: Wendy Jacobs was elected Vice Chair on a 3-2 vote.

conflicts.issue: Phased Grading Acreage Limits, Tree Preservation Tiers, and Enforcement in UDO Text Amendment 23-0687 (TC2200004)
conflicts.summary: The board split 3-2 over UDO Text Amendment TC2200004, debating whether a 50-acre phase cap and tiered tree-preservation rules went far enough to curb mass grading, buffer clearing, and sediment runoff into Lick Creek.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve TC2200004 as an immediate step forward that prevents unphased clear-cutting, avoids high-density loopholes, and can be strengthened during the UDO rewrite.
side_a_arguments: Requiring tree preservation within each phase prevents developers from clear-cutting an entire 50+ acre tract at once and clustering saved trees on one edge.
Unlike Cary's three-tier rule that exempts developments above 8 dwelling units per acre from grading limits, Durham's rule applies across all applicable projects.
City Council already passed the amendment unanimously, and rejecting or delaying it would postpone environmental protections while staff prepares the UDO rewrite.
conflicts.side_b_position: Dissent against adopting TC2200004 as drafted (2 nay votes on voice vote), arguing the 50-acre phase cap and enforcement mechanisms fail to match stricter peer limits or stop developer damage.
side_b_arguments: Commissioner Burns questioned why Durham allowed 50-acre phases rather than adopting the 20–25 acre mass-grading limits used by Cary, Raleigh, or Wake Forest.
Critics and public speakers pointed to continued sediment runoff into Lick Creek, utility/buffer disturbance exceptions, and perceived delays in enforcement despite added county inspection positions.
conflicts.resolution: Both TC2200004 (23-0687) and its NCGS 160D-605 consistency statement passed 3-2 on voice votes.

conflicts.issue: Delays and Equity in Approving COVID-19 Employee Compensation / Differential Pay
conflicts.summary: Commissioner Nimasheena Burns sharply criticized repeated board delays and questioning over compensating frontline county staff during the pandemic, contrasting that scrutiny with quick approvals for other projects, while colleagues sought FEMA-reimbursement clarity and deferred action to the budget retreat.
conflicts.side_a_position: Move decisively to compensate frontline employees who worked long hours without raises during COVID-19 rather than repeatedly delaying while other projects receive unquestioned funding.
side_a_arguments: Frontline staff worked 12- to 20-hour days without raises for over a year while board members continually asked for more analysis.
Certain county initiatives such as TIF projects and task forces receive funding with minimal scrutiny, making employee compensation an issue of labor equity.
Targeting FEMA 75% reimbursable differential pay rather than the non-reimbursable 5% option is fiscally responsible.
conflicts.side_b_position: Review financial options carefully—including FEMA reimbursement eligibility, liability-free leave alternatives, and broad staff vs. AMI criteria—and defer detailed deliberation to the February 23-24 Budget Retreat.
side_b_arguments: Understanding the difference between differential pay, non-expiring leave liability, and COLA impacts is necessary before adopting a policy.
The board was scheduled to begin a day-and-a-half budget retreat the following morning where full budget trade-offs would be examined.
conflicts.resolution: No vote was taken on February 22; commissioners agreed to carry detailed questions into the February 23-25 Budget Retreat (and subsequently approved 10% FEMA-reimbursable differential pay on March 22).

conflicts.issue: Southeast Durham Watershed Improvement Plan Scope vs. Resident Demands for Development Moratorium (Item 24-0076)
conflicts.summary: Public commenters and Vice Chair Burns questioned whether approving a $91,900 watershed planning agreement addressed urgent stormwater pollution without halting high-density construction in Southeast Durham.
conflicts.side_a_position: Residents need immediate regulatory relief—including a moratorium on high-density development—and guaranteed community participation rather than merely commissioning another planning study.
side_a_arguments: Speakers cited elevated sediment and chlorophyll-a levels in Little Lick Creek and Falls Lake alongside roughly 37,000 incoming residents.
Vice Chair Burns questioned moving forward without direct resident relief and demanded verifiable outreach to impacted neighborhoods.
conflicts.side_b_position: Approve the $91,900 City-County interlocal agreement now so technical watershed analysis and formal community outreach can proceed.
side_b_arguments: Staff and Commissioner Jacobs clarified the contract itself funds the watershed improvement plan and structured stakeholder engagement.
Completing the joint study equips the City and County with actionable engineering and policy recommendations.
conflicts.resolution: Following clarifications on community engagement scope, the Board voted unanimously 5-0 to approve item 24-0076.

conflicts.issue: Continuance vs. Immediate Quasi-Judicial Decision on Mason Farms Community Wastewater Permit (M220001)
conflicts.summary: Following neighbor testimony protesting a broken City website link on the mailed public notice and unfamiliarity with quasi-judicial expert-witness rules, Chair Brenda A. Howerton read an attorney-prepared draft continuance to November 14, 2022, triggering board debate over whether continuing the hearing was legally appropriate or fair to all parties.
conflicts.side_a_position: Continue the quasi-judicial hearing (for 30 to 60 days) to allow neighboring residents time to review documents and retain experts given notice confusion.
side_a_arguments: The mailed notice letter directed residents to an incorrect City URL, creating barriers to accessing staff materials prior to the hearing.
Neighbors unfamiliar with quasi-judicial evidentiary rules requested additional time to consult wastewater and hydrology experts.
conflicts.side_b_position: Proceed to vote immediately on the closed evidentiary record because all legal notice requirements and UDO review factors were satisfied.
side_b_arguments: Planning Director Sara Young confirmed the broken URL was not a statutory or UDO notice defect, and the applicant already held an extended hearing with sworn experts.
Under quasi-judicial law, if competent, substantial evidence meets every UDO standard and no rebuttal expert evidence exists, the Board cannot deny or delay merely out of neighborhood opposition.
conflicts.resolution: After legal counsel advised putting a motion on the floor to vote up or down, Commissioner Carter moved approval of M220001, Commissioner Jacobs came around to the UDO standard, and the Board voted 5-0 to approve both M220001 and D2100325 without a continuance.

conflicts.issue: Durham County Youth Home Construction Financing and Contract (Item 21-0715) vs. Six-Month Delay for Community Alternatives
conflicts.summary: Public commenters and the Community Safety and Wellness Task Force urged a six-month delay on Youth Home construction contracts to redirect funds toward community-based alternatives, while all five commissioners ultimately voted to proceed with the replacement facility alongside future prevention dialogue.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the Youth Home project ordinance and construction contract immediately to replace an outdated detention site with a trauma-informed, programming-focused Youth Assessment Center.
side_a_arguments: State law requires secure detention housing for court-remanded youth; delaying the project risks leaving youth in substandard facilities or shipping them out of county.
The new facility allocates over 27,500 square feet to therapeutic assessment, schooling, counseling, and family engagement, supported by juvenile justice leaders including Rep. Marcia Morey.
Commissioners argued the county must invest in both community prevention and humane statutorily required care rather than treating them as mutually exclusive.
conflicts.side_b_position: Delay Youth Home financing and construction contracts for six months to evaluate non-carceral youth investments and expand community input.
side_b_arguments: All 114 written public comments read into the record and the Community Safety and Wellness Task Force urged a six-month moratorium under the principle that 'youth heal in communities, not cages.'
Opponents questioned statutory necessity for the 36-bed size and argued $29.97M in debt could better address root causes of youth justice involvement.
conflicts.resolution: The board voted 5-0 to approve Item 21-0715; Commissioner Heidi Carter also proposed a follow-up motion on future community youth-investment engagement, which Chair Howerton deferred to a subsequent meeting.

conflicts.issue: Board Training Consultant Selection and Solicitation of Additional Proposals
conflicts.summary: Commissioners split 4-1 over whether to accept or solicit two competing consultant bids alongside the existing 'Bob' group proposal for board governance and dissent-management training.
conflicts.side_a_position: Commit to board training on group norms, rules of engagement, and managing dissent, and instruct the County Attorney to bring back two additional consultant options/bids before selecting a vendor.
side_a_arguments: Having two additional options alongside the Bob group proposal ensures a sound, competitive selection process.
The board should collaboratively define its training topics and scope of work.
conflicts.side_b_position: Proceed without delaying or subjecting the current MWBE-linked consultant team to additional late objections that should have been sent to the attorney beforehand.
side_b_arguments: Commissioners had prior opportunities to submit questions and concerns in advance rather than objecting publicly with consultants on the line.
Delaying an already-presented customized proposal undermines good-faith outreach to the invited consultants.
conflicts.resolution: Motion passed 4-1 directing Attorney Siler to return with two additional consultant options.

conflicts.issue: County Input Process and Citizen Hearing Rights on Municipal Annexations
conflicts.summary: Following public comment opposing reduced county oversight of city annexations, commissioners disagreed on whether shifting to informational-only work-session reviews for out-of-UGB annexations adequately protected unincorporated county residents.
conflicts.side_a_position: Formalize BOCC work-session informational reviews for annexations outside the Urban Growth Boundary and forward written commissioner comments to City Council, while keeping JCCPC summary reports for inconsistent in-UGB rezonings.
side_a_arguments: The County lacks legal jurisdiction over municipal annexations, so holding a formal public hearing at the BOCC risks creating the legal illusion of county decision-making authority.

Replacing ad-hoc staff emails with structured work-session presentations and written commissioner comment sheets will actually increase commissioner preparation and formal record input to City Council.
conflicts.side_b_position: Reject limiting BOCC annexation reviews to informational work-session items where residents cannot speak during an item-specific public hearing.
side_b_arguments: Unincorporated county residents cannot vote for City Council and rely on the BOCC as their only elected voice when adjacent city annexations cause flooding or blasting damage.
Discontinuing formal public hearings on annexation cases effectively removes residents' opportunity to speak directly to the Board on specific projects.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote taken at the work session; Planning Director Sara Young agreed to retain JCCPC summary reports highlighting inconsistent rezonings inside the UGB, drop the periodic comment emails, and prepare written commissioner comment sheets for future out-of-UGB work-session items ahead of the next JCCPC meeting.

conflicts.issue: Rent Subsidies vs. Binding Affordability Mandates for 300 E. Main St. Childcare Operator
conflicts.summary: Commissioners clashed over how to balance nonprofit/for-profit operator selection, below-market lease terms, and guaranteed affordable childcare slots at the 300 E. Main St. county complex.
conflicts.side_a_position: Oppose ongoing county rent subsidies given $2M+ already committed to the lease/buildout, and enforce strict sliding-scale and voucher seat percentages directly in the lease.
side_a_arguments: Durham County is already paying roughly $176,000/year plus 2% annual escalations over 15 years, making nominal rent an inappropriate precedent.
County Attorney Curtis Massey advised that nominal or below-market rent legally requires binding public-purpose restrictions such as sliding-scale or voucher quotas rather than mere 501(c)(3) status.
Commissioners Carter and Allam stressed that guaranteeing affordable seats for low-income families must remain central despite $300k–$500k+ upfit costs above the developer allowance.
conflicts.side_b_position: Avoid changing procurement expectations retroactively after inviting for-profit applicants and evaluate concrete subsidy-to-seat tradeoffs before locking in requirements.
side_b_arguments: If nonprofit-only operation was a mandatory condition, the County and CCSA should have restricted the RFP upfront rather than shortlisting three for-profit finalists.
Upfit costs of $300k–$500k+ affect whether any operator can sustain high affordable-seat quotas without lease or capital assistance.
conflicts.resolution: Staff and CCSA were directed to return to the Board with structured lease, upfit, and sliding-scale/voucher seat scenarios.

conflicts.issue: Off-Cycle Preconstruction Capital Requests vs. Comprehensive CIP Review (Items 24-0179 and 24-0183)
conflicts.summary: Commissioners pushed back against placing ad-hoc facility and preconstruction items on the consent agenda outside the formal annual Capital Improvement Plan prioritization process.
conflicts.side_a_position: Pause standalone preconstruction and renovation items (24-0179 Sheriff's Training Facility $350k and 24-0183 Project BUILD $200k) until the Board conducts full CIP and budget deliberations.
side_a_arguments: Approving individual capital preconstruction requests piecemeal bypasses Board ranking against long-waiting priorities such as the animal shelter (delayed 12 years).
Deferring items to budget/CIP work sessions allows commissioners to weigh total capital capacity and site readiness together.
conflicts.side_b_position: Bring forward time-sensitive departmental facility and partner space needs for early preconstruction authorization as they arise.
side_b_arguments: Advancing design and preconstruction prevents delays on active public safety and youth-intervention programs.
conflicts.resolution: Staff agreed to pause item 24-0179 until CIP/budget review and hold item 24-0183 for May work session discussion.

conflicts.issue: Adoption of Privately Initiated SCAD UDO Text Amendment (23-0896)
conflicts.summary: Commissioners split 3-1 over adopting the City Council-amended Simplifying Codes for Affordable Development (SCAD) UDO text amendment, debating joint City-County UDO uniformity, ADU and parking rules, and whether privately initiated text amendments should wait for the comprehensive UDO rewrite.
conflicts.side_a_position: Adopt the City Council-modified SCAD amendment to keep a unified City-County UDO, expand ADUs and remove parking minimums, and monitor impacts during the UDO rewrite.
side_a_arguments: Voting no would split the shared UDO into separate City and County ordinances for the first time.

City Council removed the provisions Planning staff flagged as problematic, and remaining items like larger ADUs (above 800 sq ft) and ADUs on church property help county residents and aging family members.
Removing parking minimums reduces car dependency and supports walkability and transit, while staff will monitor unintended impacts ahead of the UDO rewrite.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose adopting the privately initiated SCAD amendment prior to the comprehensive UDO rewrite.
side_b_arguments: As chair of the Joint City-County Planning Committee, Burns recalled near-unanimous agreement to limit private text amendments until the comprehensive UDO rewrite was completed.
Most provisions primarily affect the City rather than unincorporated Durham County, and ADU amendments had already been passed previously.
Rejected political pressure from external advocates and argued the amendment did not meaningfully guarantee affordable housing.
conflicts.resolution: Both the ordinance (23-0896) and its statutory consistency statement passed 3-1 (Allam, Jacobs, Carter aye; Burns nay).

conflicts.meeting_title: Board of County Commissioners - Budget Work Session #4 (June 5, 2023)
conflicts.issue: Boys & Girls Club $80,000 Van Request and Nonprofit Vetting Integrity in the Add/Delete Process
conflicts.summary: A sharp disagreement broke out over Chair Brenda A. Howerton's push to insert $80,000 for two Boys and Girls Club transport vans into the budget add/delete list, with three commissioners warning the request bypassed departmental nonprofit vetting.
conflicts.side_a_position: Do not insert unvetted mid-budget nonprofit requests onto the add/delete list outside established departmental and subject-matter-expert review.
side_a_arguments: Bypassing competitive grants and staff vetting sets a precedent that politicizes the add/delete process and creates inequities among worthy local nonprofits.
Requests from outside organizations must run through consistent formal policy criteria and ARPA/surplus channels rather than last-minute commissioner add-ons.
conflicts.side_b_position: Act urgently to fund two vans for the Boys and Girls Club so vulnerable Durham Public Schools students have safe transportation to after-school programming.
side_b_arguments: The Boys and Girls Club's existing vans are deteriorating and urgent youth transportation needs cannot wait until another budget cycle.
With only weeks left before adoption, commissioners must find an immediate way to support children already served by DPS.
conflicts.resolution: Although Commissioner Carter briefly offered collegial compromise, commissioners reached consensus not to insert the $80,000 into the general operating add/delete list, instead directing County Manager Sowell to explore surplus county vans or ARPA options and establish a clear nonprofit budget-request policy.

conflicts.issue: Scheduling the Museum of Durham History Funding Presentation for the June 5 Budget Work Session
conflicts.summary: Commissioners and County Management disagreed on whether to place the Museum of Durham History's expansion and salary funding request on the June 5 final budget work session agenda before the City of Durham had acted on the joint request.
conflicts.side_a_position: Hear a 30-minute informational presentation from the Museum of Durham History at the June 5 work session so the full board can review the request before the July recess.
side_a_arguments: Not all commissioners have received the background information shared with the museum liaison, and the next regular work session after June is not until August due to the July break.
Joint City-County meetings do not include the full Board of County Commissioners, and Council Member Williams had already asked about it on the City side.
A 30-minute slot was open in the June 5 afternoon schedule.
conflicts.side_b_position: Defer joint City-County funding requests like the Museum of Durham History to the June 13 Joint City-County meeting rather than placing unvetted joint asks on the June 5 budget wrap-up session.
side_b_arguments: Budget work sessions are intended for items the County will fund wholly and decide upon for the June 12 budget adoption, whereas the City budget office received the request late and was not considering it yet.
Making a County budget commitment or add/delete decision on June 5 without knowing the City's position would be premature, and any post-June 12 funding would require August fund balance action.
conflicts.resolution: Commissioners agreed to accommodate a strictly 30-minute informational presentation on June 5 while deferring any joint funding coordination to the June 13 Joint City-County meeting.

conflicts.issue: Adding Late Presentations (Museum of Durham History, Lebanon Fire District) and Potentially Using June 6 for Budget Work Sessions
conflicts.summary: Commissioners differed over whether to add non-tax-rate or late-submitted presentations onto the June 1 and June 5 budget work sessions or extend deliberations to the reserved June 6 date.
conflicts.side_a_position: Add timely informational updates such as the Lebanon Fire District staffing transition and Museum of Durham History to upcoming work sessions, and ensure Low-Income Homeowner Relief policy changes come to the full BOCC first.
side_a_arguments: Residents in the Lebanon Fire District are alarmed about full-time firefighters being let go and potential impacts on response and homeowners insurance ratings.
The full BOCC does not attend Joint City-County meetings, so board members need direct briefings on policies they must approve.
conflicts.side_b_position: Keep the June 1 and June 5 budget work sessions strictly focused on county budget decisions and honor the pre-scheduled calendar without spilling over to June 6.
side_b_arguments: The board already faces 7.5-hour budget work session days, and adding 30- to 45-minute late requests from external groups is unfair to budget staff and other presenters.
Budget dates have been on the calendar since the start of the year and should be honored rather than forcing staff and commissioners back on June 6.
conflicts.resolution: Staff noted Lebanon Fire District had no tax rate increase and would be placed on a regular work session after the budget, Low-Income Homeowner Relief policy updates would return to the full board without affecting the budget allocation, and the pre-set June 1 and June 5 schedule was maintained.

conflicts.issue: Durham Inclusion in Phase 1 vs. Alternative Investments for the Greater Triangle Commuter Rail Study
conflicts.summary: Following GoTriangle's report that full West Durham-to-Garner/Clayton commuter rail costs jumped 50% to $2.8B-$3.2B, commissioners clashed over GoTriangle's proposed starter-phase options, private-sector/business displacement concerns, and whether commuter rail remains viable compared with Bus Rapid Transit and local micro-transit.
conflicts.side_a_position: Durham County must be included in any Phase 1 corridor with Wake County (not Johnston County first), with aggressive federal IIJA/FRA grant pursuit and private-sector/RTP funding participation.
side_a_arguments: Durham taxpayers passed the half-cent transit sales tax long ago while Johnston County has no dedicated transit tax.
With 2050 traffic maps turning solid red and regional job growth concentrating east of Durham, leaving Durham residents out of Phase 1 would cut them off from economic mobility.
Staff and GoTriangle must pursue 80/20 federal Rail Crossing Elimination grants immediately and bring RTP/business leaders into early co-funding talks.
conflicts.side_b_position: Question high Durham-segment costs ($1.6B), Driver Street small Black business displacement, lack of complete federal funding plans, and whether $3.2B-scale spending would be better directed to BRT and localized rapid transit.
side_b_arguments: Commissioners need a full menu of feasible federal funding pots before committing, as current revenue appears insufficient for a $2.8B-$3.2B build.
East Durham's Driver Street corridor contains roughly seven small Black-owned businesses that could be harmed by host-railroad crossing closures.
Localized micro-transit or Bus Rapid Transit along corridors like 15-501 and West Durham-Ellis Road may serve Durham's near-term needs better than relying on long commuter lines.
conflicts.resolution: Informational discussion concluded without a vote; GoTriangle committed to bring back a federal grant matrix and conduct a 45-day public engagement period, while County staff scheduled a Durham Transit Plan update for October.

conflicts.issue: Rationale and Equity of Commuter Rail Investments vs. Local Bus and Micro-Transit Priorities
conflicts.summary: Following Triangle J COG's Opportunity Analysis briefing, Commissioner Nimasheena Burns challenged the equity rationale for prioritizing expensive commuter rail over local bus service, while Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs and Chair Brenda A. Howerton emphasized regional job connectivity and public-private transit-oriented development.
conflicts.side_a_position: Pursue a regional multimodal rail spine paired with public-private TOD partnerships and dedicated first-mile/last-mile connectors so Durham residents can reach Triangle job centers.
side_a_arguments: Eight of the region's top ten job hubs, major universities, and 37% of Durham's legally restricted affordable housing lie within the corridor.
South Florida's Tri-Rail and Brightline demonstrate that electric shuttles, joint development value capture, and multi-county alignment can serve both riders and regional growth.
conflicts.side_b_position: Question whether commuter rail serves low-income bus riders earning under $40,000 or leaves behind local bus rapid transit and neighborhood bus connections.
side_b_arguments: Few of the 9,000 downtown apartments or corridor jobs serve very-low-income residents without guaranteed affordable fares and simultaneous BRT/feeder investments.
Commissioners remain skeptical that four separate governments will build feeder bus rapid transit in tandem with rail, risking low-income neighborhoods being left behind.
conflicts.resolution: Informational discussion ended without a vote; staff noted the Durham County Transit Plan update later in 2022 would weigh both bus and commuter rail allocations.

conflicts.issue: Durham County Transit Plan: City Staffing/Sidewalk Cost-Sharing vs. Utilizing $100M Transit Fund Balance
conflicts.summary: Commissioners and City/County transportation leaders disagreed over whether to require City of Durham cost-sharing for additional transit project-delivery staff and sidewalk improvements, and whether the accumulated ~$87–$100 million half-cent transit sales tax fund balance should be tapped to accelerate local bus/access projects or preserved for major regional transit investments.
conflicts.side_a_position: Require City cost-sharing for City transit staff and sidewalk improvements, establish clear tri-board financial/governance policies with GoTriangle, and preserve the transit sales tax fund balance for regional commuter rail or Bus Rapid Transit (BRT).
side_a_arguments: Durham County generates only ~$30–$32 million/year in transit revenues (potentially losing ~$25 million over 20 years from rental-car tax changes), so sidewalk repairs and amenities—basic city functions—should not crowd out core transit service and regional BRT/rail (Jacobs, Carter).
The ~$87–$100 million fund balance exists specifically because voters approved the sales tax for major regional projects like commuter rail (Jacobs).
Cost-sharing ensures 'skin in the game' and clear governance policies among the County, City, and GoTriangle (Howerton, Jacobs, County Manager staff Ellen Beckman).
conflicts.side_b_position: Support funding requested City transit staff positions without punitive cost-share delays and leverage the ~$100 million transit fund balance to deliver overdue bus stop, sidewalk, and corridor improvements immediately.
side_b_arguments: Without additional staffing capacity, $25–$35 million in transit corridor projects face 8%–10% annual construction cost escalation (~$1 million/year lost per year of delay) while transit-dependent riders (80% people of color, two-thirds zero-car households) wait for basic shelters and sidewalks (City Director Sean Egan, Bike Durham).
Approving requested staffing positions is critical so historically excluded neighborhoods do not remain left behind on overdue transit and shelter repairs (Allam).
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote was taken at the work session; Chair Howerton requested GoTriangle fund-balance documentation and staff continued developing formal cost-sharing and governance policies through the tri-board governance study.

conflicts.issue: DPS Additional $2M Operating Request, Enrollment Decline, and Inter-Board Communication
conflicts.summary: Commissioners challenged DPS leadership over its request for $2-$3 million above the County Manager's $9.875 million increase recommendation amid declining enrollment and frustration with School Board members' public messaging and lack of direct outreach.
conflicts.side_a_position: Question additional ongoing funding above the Manager's $9.875M (+9% per-pupil) recommendation without clearer accountability on declining enrollment (~1,055 drop), classified/certified wage sustainability, and direct School Board communication.
side_a_arguments: Commissioner Nimasheena Burns rebuked School Board members for never contacting commissioners directly while alleging BOCC lacked commitment to DPS teachers and staff.
Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs noted DPS enrollment fell from 32,596 in FY19-20 to ~31,300 projected while county per-pupil funding rose to $4,333.
Chair Brenda A. Howerton stressed fiduciary duty to avoid unnecessary tax hikes amid inflation and warned against shifting narratives when BOCC asks accountability questions.
conflicts.side_b_position: Fund DPS's revised $11.875M essential local operating need (absorbing ~$1M in IT technicians and Lyons Farm expansion internally) to cover fixed costs, teacher salary supplements ($6,500 minimum), and post-pandemic student supports.
side_b_arguments: Superintendent Pascal Mubenga explained pre-pandemic growth reversed by ~1,300 students statewide due to COVID-19 and projected 20,000 more school-age children over five years, noting county dollars fund summer counselors and intensive behavioral COPE staffing (~6-7 adults per 18 students) uncovered by the state.
CFO Paul LeSieur noted charter pass-throughs (+$1.97M/+2.6M) consume substantial local increases and recurring fund balance use is unsustainable.

Commissioner Heidi Carter expressed support for meeting the $11.8M adjusted request while calling for a county-city-DPS community conversation on a sustainable living wage for over 1,000 low-paid school employees.
conflicts.resolution: Vice Chair Jacobs indicated consensus to examine funding DPS's revised $11.8M request while County Manager Kimberly Sowell asked DPS for eight-year enrollment trajectories and charter/fund-balance absorption options before budget adoption.

conflicts.issue: Transit Plan Governance Prior-Approval Authority and FY23 City/GoTriangle FTE Deferrals
conflicts.summary: GoTriangle registered minority opposition in joint workshops to giving BOCC prior approval/veto power over the annual transit budget, while Durham commissioners strongly backed increased oversight and supported deferring 3.25 requested City/GoTriangle FTEs.
conflicts.side_a_position: Grant the BOCC primary approval authority over the annual transit work program prior to GoTriangle board action, and defer City (3 FTE) and GoTriangle (0.25 FTE) requests until a formal ILA and cost-share agreement are adopted.
side_a_arguments: County staff (Ellen Beckman) and Commissioners Burns, Carter, and Howerton argued BOCC currently has zero formal budget vote despite levying the transit tax and faces unclear City/County/GoTriangle project responsibilities.
Staff noted deferring the 3.25 FTEs ensures clearer scope accountability on corridor projects (Fayetteville/Holloway) and establishes whether Durham or transit funds pay City staffing.
conflicts.side_b_position: Retain GoTriangle/transit-operator-led timeline sequencing and approve requested City/GoTriangle staffing immediately.
side_b_arguments: GoTriangle expressed minority concern that sequential BOCC approval before GoTriangle board adoption could compress fiscal-year deadlines.
Public commenter Eric Landfried urged approving the City's 3 FTEs now to speed bus and station delivery.
conflicts.resolution: Commissioners endorsed staff's governance recommendations for ILA drafting and scheduled formal FY23 Work Program comments for adoption on May 9.

conflicts.issue: Action Timeline vs. Budget Process for Black Maternal Health Community Commitments
conflicts.summary: Black maternal health CBO leaders and Commissioner Nimasheena Burns demanded concrete funding commitments after nearly a year of meetings without action, while Chair Brenda A. Howerton and other commissioners insisted requests proceed through staff vetting and the FY 2022-23 budget cycle.
conflicts.side_a_position: Move beyond repeated presentations to immediate, written financial and programmatic commitments from the county.
side_a_arguments: Commissioner Nimasheena Burns noted commissioners heard similar recommendations on June 3, 2021 and already identified $1 million in mental-health funds, arguing 'we are not going to keep meeting about babies' while infants and mothers die.
Joy Spencer (Equity Before Birth) stated organizations had met tirelessly with zero formal written 'yes' or operational commitments.
conflicts.side_b_position: Channel specific CBO budget requests through GM Joanne Pierce and County Manager Sowell for formal consideration during upcoming FY 2022-23 budget adoption rather than making work-session commitments.
side_b_arguments: Chair Brenda A. Howerton stated work sessions are informational only and directed CBOs to present concise, prioritized asks to GM Pierce so the Board understands exact dollar needs and funding offsets.
Commissioners Heidi Carter and Wendy Jacobs affirmed strong support for both Public Health's specific FY23 requests and breaking down departmental silos during the impending budget markup.
conflicts.resolution: Chair Howerton secured agreement from presenters to meet immediately with GM Joanne Pierce to formulate concrete budget-ready proposals.

conflicts.issue: Greater Triangle Commuter Rail Equity Priorities vs. Local Bus and Affordability Needs
conflicts.summary: Commissioners debated whether investing heavily in regional commuter rail serves low-income Durham bus riders equitably or risks leaving everyday local transit needs behind.
conflicts.side_a_position: Question the equity rationale of prioritizing regional commuter rail when low-income workers (~23% earning under $40,000 in the corridor) depend on buses and BRT has yet to be built first.
side_a_arguments: Commissioner Nimasheena Burns noted of 9,000 new downtown families cited by business leaders fewer than 1,000 are low-income and doubted poor Durham residents could afford or access rail stops before BRT and basic bus routes are delivered.
Chair Brenda A. Howerton questioned ongoing local maintenance liabilities and whether commuter rail would crowd out buses if federal dollars fall short.
conflicts.side_b_position: Pursue commuter rail alongside bus/first-mile networks as a long-term regional economic mobility spine tying Durham residents to RTP and Wake County job centers.
side_b_arguments: TJCOG's John Hodges-Koppel pointed to 70,000 BIPOC/low-income/zero-car residents near the rail spine and cited South Florida's Tri-Rail usage by service workers as evidence buses alone cannot match rail travel times through highway congestion.

Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs emphasized public-private partnerships, 37% of Durham's legally binding affordable housing lying near the corridor, and 120,000 daily inbound commuters requiring integrated regional planning.
conflicts.resolution: GoTriangle and TJCOG committed to publishing station-level maps overlaying existing/proposed bus routes, bike racks, and park-and-ride plans for ongoing Board evaluation.

conflicts.issue: Long-Term Funding Responsibility and Tax Impact of Durham Pre-K Expansion
conflicts.summary: During the Durham Pre-K quarterly update, commissioners disagreed over how to sustainably finance universal preschool expansion beyond 2026 ARPA deadlines and whether Durham Public Schools should bear half the cost.
conflicts.side_a_position: Require Durham Public Schools to fund 50% of Pre-K expansion from its ARPA/ESSER allocations and weigh Durham's higher property tax rate relative to Wake and Mecklenburg counties before committing post-2026 recurring County dollars.
side_a_arguments: ARPA funds must be obligated by 2024 and spent by 2026, creating a recurring funding cliff in 2027-2029 that could force local property tax increases when Durham's tax rate already exceeds Charlotte and Wake County.
Durham Public Schools received substantial ESSER and ARPA funds and should share 50% of expansion costs rather than placing the burden solely on the County.
Commissioners should not compare votes on unrelated issues to question board members' commitment to early childhood education.
conflicts.side_b_position: Prioritize Durham Pre-K as the County's top evidence-based investment using ARPA and local budget planning to move steadily toward the 3,268-seat universal goal.
side_b_arguments: Early childhood investment is the County's most effective systemic strategy for long-term educational equity, violence prevention, and workforce support.
With 1,516 of 3,268 target seats currently funded, the board must commit to a multi-year growth trajectory and build evaluation and prenatal-to-three capacity.
No other commissioners nodded in support when asked to commit to demanding a 50% funding match from Durham Public Schools.
conflicts.resolution: Informational discussion only with no vote taken; Interim Manager Claudia Hager committed to balancing one-time ARPA investments with long-term recurring budget strategies ahead of FY23 budget deliberations.

conflicts.issue: BOCC–Durham Public Schools MOU: Funding Matrix Removal, Reporting Deadlines, and Board-to-Board Communication (Item 21-0682)
conflicts.summary: Reviewing DPS's proposed 2021 MOU edits, staff and commissioners supported rejecting a fixed funding matrix and local funding mandate clause while debating fixed annual reporting dates and direct commissioner-to-school-board communication ahead of the joint meeting.
conflicts.side_a_position: Strike the fixed funding formula matrix and local-responsibility clause, add explicit Universal Pre-K and fixed annual reporting deadlines to ensure accountability.
side_a_arguments: Interim Manager Claudia Hager, Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs, and Commissioner Heidi Carter warned a strict property/sales tax formula risks automatic per-pupil cuts during downturns and obscures the State's constitutional school funding role.
Vice Chair Jacobs urged embedding Universal Pre-K language and definite annual report deadlines so previous 2017 reporting commitments do not go unfulfilled.
conflicts.side_b_position: Avoid overly rigid staff reporting calendar mandates and share proposed BOCC revisions directly with School Board liaisons rather than routing unilateral edits solely through staff.
side_b_arguments: Commissioner Nimasheena Burns criticized lacking prior committee updates and urged commissioners to communicate suggested revisions directly with DPS board members so they are not surprised at the joint meeting.
Chair Brenda A. Howerton cautioned against writing rigid report dates into the MOU that might burden staff when DPS annual data arrives on variable schedules.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote was taken; Interim Manager Hager committed to softening exact reporting-date language to an annual presentation and sharing updated draft edits with the DPS Superintendent and School Board ahead of the joint meeting.

conflicts.issue: Food Security $10.1M ARPA Proposals: Urgent Stop-Gap Relief vs. Process Rigor, BIPOC Farmer Access, and DPS ESSER Overlap
conflicts.summary: Commissioners and staff debated how to balance urgent $8.6 million food-security and school kitchen equipment funding requests against limited ARPA dollars, uniform procurement rules, and concerns over whether Black farmers and businesses could actually qualify.
conflicts.side_a_position: Subject all $10.1M in food security proposals to the county's uniform ARPA rubric, RFP competition, disaggregated equity verification, and scrutiny of school vs. county funding sources.
side_a_arguments: Commissioner Nimasheena Burns questioned how Black farmers could benefit when only one Black farmer in the county is GAP/GHP certified, and urged checking whether DPS should pay for its $4.5M kitchen equipment needs from its $146M in ESSER funds.

Chair Brenda Howerton called for disaggregated data rather than broad promises that funds will help Black residents, stressing the board must allow the County Manager to evaluate all competing requests strategically.

Interim Manager Claudia Hager and Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs emphasized that $62.4M in ARPA cannot cover every ask and all proposals must pass compliance, RFP, and rubric vetting alongside upcoming housing proposals.
conflicts.side_b_position: Prioritize immediate stop-gap emergency food grants and produce boxes quickly, potentially via fund balance or FEMA reimbursement, while using RFPs and non-GAP-restricted grants to reach BIPOC partners.
side_b_arguments: Commissioner Heidi Carter argued 'stop-gap' emergency food grants for existing distributors like the Food Security Task Force and Congregations in Action should come forward expeditiously, even using fund balance subject to reimbursement.

Mary Oxendine clarified that GAP certification is only required for selling to schools—not for the proposed produce box or farmer grants—and offered to return in the emergency-operations channel to prevent a lapse in produce boxes.

DPS Child Nutrition Director Jim Keaton explained that child nutrition operates as a self-funded enterprise fund strained by lower virtual-school meal reimbursements and $15/hour county-aligned wages.
conflicts.resolution: No funding vote was taken; Chair Howerton directed Interim Manager Hager and staff to review all requests under the county's compliance and rubric framework and schedule follow-up one-on-one and board discussions.

conflicts.issue: Board Training Consultant Proposal Scope, Cost, and Board Involvement
conflicts.summary: Commissioners debated the scope, cost, timeframe, and fairness of the board training consultant proposal process, as well as limited initial slots for Racial Equity Institute training.
conflicts.side_a_position: Question the consultant proposal's cost, timeframe, and scope of work, ensure all five board members have direct input, and explore less expensive public/nonprofit alternatives such as UNC School of Government or Racial Equity Institute.
side_a_arguments: All five commissioners should help define the training scope of work rather than relying on a process where only two commissioners were initially involved.
Public or nonprofit providers may offer lower-cost options, and all commissioners should have access to racial equity training slots.
conflicts.side_b_position: Defend the timeline and clerk's recordkeeping on prior discussions and training registration, and move expeditiously so consultants are not left waiting.
side_b_arguments: The clerk maintained attendance records of prior conversations and registered commissioners for racial equity training in the order responses arrived.
The newly sworn-in board had discussed spring training since February and owed the consultants timely clarity.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote was taken; after closed session, Chair Howerton directed commissioners to email questions, concerns, or decisions to the County Attorney within the week.

conflicts.meeting_title: Board of County Commissioners - FY 2024-25 Budget Work Session #4 - Wednesday, June 4, 2024
conflicts.issue: FY 2024-25 Property Tax Burden and Durham Public Schools Funding Accountability
conflicts.summary: Commissioners split sharply in tone and assessment over the proposed FY 2024-25 budget compromise, weighing tax impacts on lower-income residents and DPS governance concerns against urgent school funding needs.
conflicts.side_a_position: Express deep dissatisfaction with the tax burden on low-to-middle-income residents and skepticism over DPS outcomes despite record funding
side_a_arguments: The resulting property tax increase burdens low- and middle-income households while higher-income residents are insulated.
DPS has not demonstrated a strategy to improve student outcomes next year or avoid returning with a $25M+ gap in 2025.
conflicts.side_b_position: Support the compromise school funding package as necessary crisis action while pushing for DPS accountability
side_b_arguments: Thriving public schools are essential to Durham's economy, safety, and families, requiring extraordinary action during a crisis.
Supporting the budget can coexist with demanding accountability from the School Board on child safety and financial management.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote taken at Work Session #4; County Manager Dr. Kimberly Sowell noted the compromise left everyone partly unsatisfied while minimizing the property tax rate increase ahead of the June 10 vote.

conflicts.issue: UDO Rewrite: Relaxing Density Caps for Affordability vs. High-Growth Market Reality and Rural Community Voices
conflicts.summary: Commissioners questioned Code Studio's recommendation to shift away from units-per-acre density limits toward form-based rules, disputing whether higher density reduces rents in Durham and raising concerns about Preserve Rural Durham residents not being heard.
conflicts.side_a_position: Challenged the premise that increasing residential density lowers apartment rents in booming tech markets like Durham and warned that rural and Southeast Durham residents' environmental and blasting complaints are being ignored.
side_a_arguments: In fast-growing tech hubs receiving thousands of high-paying jobs ($170k average salaries near RTP/Davis Drive), adding dense apartments has not lowered rents in Austin, Boston, Atlanta, or Silicon Valley.
Despite hiring engagement consultants, residents who bring engineers, dirty water, and blasting permit documentation are still not being heard.
Both Carter and Burns misread JCCPC's density bullet and expressed continuing concern even after staff clarification.
conflicts.side_b_position: Supported form-based design and higher density near transit as the primary strategy to improve affordability, equity, and climate outcomes.
side_b_arguments: Economic modeling showed removing units-per-acre limits and lowering parking minimums could drop modeled multiplex rents from $3,500 to $2,000/month.
Joint MPO modeling shows higher-density land use around transit reduces congestion and greenhouse gas emissions.
Prior UDO text amendments already incorporated several Preserve Rural Durham environmental proposals.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote was taken; Vice Chair Burns requested Colin Scarff email empirical examples of high-growth tech cities where increased density lowered rents, and staff committed to updating the misleading slide text.

conflicts.issue: County Service Impacts and 50/50 Funding Equity in City-County Planning Work Program (24-0232)
conflicts.summary: Commissioners challenged how city-initiated rezonings, annexations, and water/sewer extensions generate countywide infrastructure, school, and EMS demands while Durham County pays half of the joint Planning Department's budget.
conflicts.side_a_position: The joint planning model and 50/50 cost split disproportionately burden Durham County taxpayers with downstream school and public safety costs from city growth approvals.
side_a_arguments: City rezonings and annexations add students and emergency calls without matching county operational funding or direct county approval over municipal land-use cases.
Staff capacity under the 50/50 split is heavily consumed by city development cases and annexations.
conflicts.side_b_position: The FY25 work program reflects mutually adopted Comprehensive Plan priorities and balanced city-county staffing commitments under the existing interlocal framework.
side_b_arguments: The work program advances shared goals such as the UDO rewrite, Urban Growth Boundary tree canopy protection, and small area planning.
Joint planning coordinates regional standards across both jurisdictions.
conflicts.resolution: Informational work session review; commissioners signaled interest in scrutinizing county fiscal impacts and joint governance during the budget process.

conflicts.issue: MWBE Program Accountability, C2 Contractors Scope, and Goods/Services Tracking
conflicts.summary: Vice Chair Burns questioned the transparency, scope, and board oversight of C2 Contractors' MWBE consulting work, prompting defense from County Manager Sowell and Commissioners Carter and Jacobs.
conflicts.side_a_position: C2 Contractors' exact scope of work, NAICS/commodity code tracking, and regular performance reports to the Board have been unclear and insufficient given historical disparity findings.
side_a_arguments: Commissioners have not received granular, recurring reports detailing C2's scope and measurable impact across non-construction goods and services.
Without commodity-level tracking and clear accountability benchmarks, prior disparity gaps risk persisting.
conflicts.side_b_position: C2 Contractors has delivered tangible capital-project outreach and preliminary RFQ development while the County simultaneously modernizes its internal goods-and-services tracking software.
side_b_arguments: County Manager Kimberly Sowell explained C2 supported preliminary RFQ work on 220 E. Main and outreach events, while the County is launching dedicated procurement tracking software to capture goods/services data.
Commissioners Carter and Jacobs praised the bond and capital MWBE metrics and outreach progress presented.
conflicts.resolution: Informational discussion; staff noted ongoing procurement software implementation and reporting follow-up.

conflicts.meeting_title: Board of County Commissioners - Work Session for February 5, 2024
conflicts.issue: Durham Affordable Housing Loan Fund: Affordability Deed-Restriction Terms and County Fund Structure
conflicts.summary: Commissioners differed during the ARPA/Self-Help Credit Union presentation over whether public dollars in the loan fund should require strict 30-year affordability and right-of-first-refusal terms versus more flexible 10-to-20-year restrictions to attract developers, and whether Durham County should invest directly in the existing City/Self-Help loan fund or launch a separate county RFP and fund.
conflicts.side_a_position: Require long-term (30-year) affordability restrictions and public right of first refusal, and contribute non-ARPA county dollars directly to the existing City/Self-Help fund rather than creating a separate fund.
side_a_arguments: 10-year affordability periods on public investments are insufficient and risk losing affordable units back to market rate.
Contributing directly to the existing City/Self-Help fund avoids duplicating administrative infrastructure.
conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain flexibility on developer restrictions to avoid deterring deals, and establish a distinct county revolving housing fund/RFP targeting $20 million.
side_b_arguments: Overly rigid restrictions can leave developers unwilling to participate, yielding zero units instead of flexible affordable units.
A dedicated county RFP/fund similar to Wake County's model can target county-specific needs and scale toward $20 million.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote taken; staff noted they would return with refined options and recommendations at a subsequent meeting.

conflicts.issue: UDO Text Amendment TC2302 (23-0783) Aligning Ordinance with Comprehensive Plan and Urban Growth Boundary Procedures
conflicts.summary: The board split 4-1 on adopting UDO Text Amendment TC2302 following public outcry over urban growth boundary expansions, Lick Creek and Falls Lake environmental impacts, and confusion over how the Comprehensive Plan had been approved on consent.
conflicts.side_a_position: Adopt TC2302 as the minimum procedural alignment needed to implement the adopted Comprehensive Plan while pursuing the UDO rewrite and blasting-permit reforms.
side_a_arguments: TC2302 only updates UDO references (Future Land Use Map to Place Type Map, biennial assessment reporting, and Downtown Design District boundaries) to match the already-adopted Comprehensive Plan.
Residents were heard on both sides of the urban growth boundary, and the Comprehensive Plan guarantees utility access and affordable housing policies in new growth areas.
Deeper zoning and conservation protections will be addressed during the upcoming UDO rewrite and City-County blasting permit review.
conflicts.side_b_position: Dissent against adopting TC2302 (1 nay vote; individual dissenter unnamed in voice vote), reflecting public concerns over overdevelopment and lack of transparency.
side_b_arguments: Public speakers opposed expanding subdivisions bisecting Lick Creek and threatening Falls Lake and Perry Farms.

Commissioners acknowledged residents did not realize they could request pulling the Comprehensive Plan from the prior consent agenda and expressed concern about missing markup/maps in the earlier packet.
conflicts.resolution: Both TC2302 (23-0783) and its NCGS 160D-605 consistency statement passed 4-1 on voice votes.

conflicts.meeting_title: Board of County Commissioners - Regular Session for Aug. 28, 2023
conflicts.issue: Procedural Rules and Term-Length Precedent for Deferring the Durham Tech Board of Trustees Appointment
conflicts.summary: During agenda adjustments, Commissioner Nida Allam moved to pull and defer the Durham Technical Community College Board of Trustees appointment from August 28 to the September 5 work session to address whether reappointing a term-limited incumbent to an expired slot yields a full term or shortened term, sparking pushback from Chair Brenda A. Howerton over past board precedent.
conflicts.side_a_position: Pull the Durham Tech appointment until September 5 so the board can examine bylaws and deliberate whether the expired/term-limited seat should be filled for a full or partial term.
side_a_arguments: No other applicants were considered for the expired term-limited seat, so the full board needs time to discuss the term-length implication before voting.
Under the current board's tenure since Commissioners Allam and Burns joined, a reappointment structured this way had not previously occurred.
conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain awareness that prior Boards of Commissioners have filled similar expired/term-limited appointments under existing bylaws and require staff to document historical precedent if delaying the vote.
side_b_arguments: While not done since the two newest commissioners took office, the board had handled similar appointments under its bylaws in earlier years.
Directed staff to pull historical records of prior appointments to inform the discussion.
conflicts.resolution: The board approved pulling the Durham Tech Board of Trustees vote to the September 5, 2023 work session, where it subsequently voted 4-0 to suspend the rules, set a two-year term, and appoint Dr. Tara Fikes.

conflicts.meeting_title: Board of County Commissioners - Regular Session for Jul. 10, 2023
conflicts.issue: Whether to Proceed With or Defer the ABC Board Appointment Pending Investigation of Website Posting Complaint
conflicts.summary: Following Jacqueline Wagstaff's citizen complaint that Durham County's website listed 'no vacancies' for the ABC Board throughout June, commissioners debated whether to hold the appointment and whether holding without immediately reopening applications accomplished fairness.
conflicts.side_a_position: Hold off on voting on the ABC Board appointment until staff investigates and verifies that the public application process was free of technical irregularities.
side_a_arguments: Deferring a single non-regulatory advisory/board appointment by one cycle preserves public trust without operational harm.
Staff needs time to verify website audit logs before finalizing an appointment rather than deciding whether to re-advertise prematurely.
conflicts.side_b_position: Questioned the utility of delaying the vote for a month unless new applications would also be accepted if warranted, while willing to defer if verification is the goal.
side_b_arguments: If applications are not reopened, holding a vote on the same applicant pool for one month may not change the substance of the complaint unless irregularities trigger re-advertising.
conflicts.resolution: Resolved by board consensus to hold the ABC Board appointment until the late August meeting pending County Attorney and Clerk verification of the online application posting, with re-advertising triggered only if irregularities were found.

conflicts.issue: Urgency of Direct County Funding Commitments for Community-Based Black Maternal Health Organizations
conflicts.summary: After community-based doula and teen-parent organizations described nearly a year of meetings without firm county commitments while Black maternal and infant outcomes worsened, commissioners differed on how quickly and concretely to respond during the work session.
conflicts.side_a_position: Defer formal funding commitments until General Manager Joanne Pierce meets with staff and CBOs to prepare concrete budget proposals.
side_a_arguments: Work sessions are designed for listening and information gathering rather than making immediate budget appropriations on the dais.
Staff and CBOs should meet offline to distill clear, succinct dollar asks ahead of the upcoming budget cycle.
conflicts.side_b_position: The Board must act urgently now rather than continuing endless meetings after already leaving a $1M mental-health commitment and last year's Hear Her recommendations unimplemented.
side_b_arguments: Babies and mothers are still dying nearly a year after the June 3, 2021 presentation without dedicated action steps.
Silos between hospital systems, Public Health, and Black-led grassroots providers cannot persist without direct funding and written County commitments.
conflicts.resolution: Chair Howerton directed General Manager Joanne Pierce to convene the CBOs and return concrete funding proposals for the upcoming FY23 budget cycle.

conflicts.issue: Immediate Permit Repeal vs. Structured Six-Month Operational Rollout for Community Cat (TNVR) Ordinance Amendment (22-0394)
conflicts.summary: Following divided public testimony from animal welfare advocates (supporting immediate TNVR), Audubon conservationists (opposing feral colonies), and Sheriff's Animal Services (warning of staffing and nuisance constraints), Commissioners Heidi Carter, Nimasheena Burns, and Wendy Jacobs debated whether to lift trapping permit restrictions immediately or establish Sheriff-agency procedures first.
conflicts.side_a_position: Immediately adopt the AWAC ordinance language lifting Sheriff trapping permit restrictions so volunteer nonprofits can begin TNVR right away while final implementation rules are refined.
side_a_arguments: APS is at full capacity and still forced to euthanize healthy cats because existing ordinance rules restrict nonprofits from conducting TNVR.
Independent nonprofits and volunteer veterinarians are ready to begin trapping, spay/neutering, and vaccinating cats immediately at no immediate County cost.
conflicts.side_b_position: Do not immediately remove trapping permits or assign open-ended responsibilities before Sheriff's Office buy-in, funding, holding space, nuisance remedies, and a firm ~6-month timeline are established.
side_b_arguments: The Sheriff's Office has already stopped trapping due to overcrowding and lacks staff/equipment; shifting work immediately to outside groups without contracts, funding, or enforceable rules creates accountability and citizen-nuisance gaps.
Open-ended 'later date' ordinance language lacks urgency—staff must set a clear ~6-month deadline (targeting early 2023) with all stakeholders at the table.
conflicts.resolution: Commissioner Carter agreed to withdraw immediate implementation in favor of a compromise motion—adopted 5-0 at 03:44:52—adopting the AWAC ordinance draft as a model and directing staff to work with the Sheriff's Office, AWAC, APS, and nonprofits to finalize procedures within roughly six months.

conflicts.issue: Triangle Bikeway Resolution: Community Engagement, Transit Equity, and Recreational Priorities (Item 22-0296)
conflicts.summary: Although the Board ultimately adopted the non-binding Triangle Bikeway resolution 5-0, Chair Howerton and Commissioner Burns challenged the sufficiency of community outreach and questioned prioritizing bike corridors over bus integration and youth ATV recreation, while Vice Chair Jacobs urged approval as a necessary first planning step.
conflicts.side_a_position: Questioned rushing forward with bike-lane resolutions without documented community-organization feedback, bus-system integration, or safe facilities for youth riding ATVs.
side_a_arguments: The packet lacked responses from most contacted community organizations aside from the Durham Committee on the Affairs of Black People (Howerton).
Bikeways do not address youth racing ATVs on highways who need safe recreational spaces (Howerton).

Roughly 80% of bus riders are not commuting 20–30 miles on dark bike trails; the Board 'rams things through' on bike lanes and must ensure intentional outreach and bus integration going forward (Burns).
conflicts.side_b_position: Approve the resolution as an essential initial regional planning step that commits zero County funding.
side_b_arguments: The resolution only endorses the regional vision so partners like Wake County, RTP Foundation, and NCDOT can explore future phased funding for the ~$63 million Durham/Orange segments.
Approving the plan is procedurally required before any future implementation or grant applications can occur.
conflicts.resolution: Staff confirmed the resolution committed no County funding and pledged to send additional outreach responses and explore ATV recreation separately; the Board approved the resolution 5-0.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Delegates Meeting with County Commissioners and Staff
conflicts.issue: DPS Educator Affordable Housing Authority (SB 203/HB 231) and Inter-Board Advocacy
conflicts.summary: Commissioner Nimasheena Burns clashed with characterizations of BOCC inaction on teacher affordable housing, while state lawmakers maintained the sole hurdle was Senate leadership despite existing statutory conveyance options.
conflicts.side_a_position: Reject claims that BOCC is blocking DPS affordable housing, question lack of active DPS lobbying in Raleigh, and pursue immediate legal verification of existing statutory authority.
side_a_arguments: Commissioner Nimasheena Burns objected to Durham County commissioners being used as a 'political punching bag' and stated she was told the School Board had not consistently lobbied legislative leadership on the bill over the prior year.
Commissioner Heidi Carter and Chair Brenda A. Howerton welcomed clarification of existing county conveyance powers so project work could proceed without waiting on Raleigh.
conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain that all local boards advocated and attribute the legislative stall solely to Senate leadership refusing local bills for teacher housing.
side_b_arguments: Sen. Mike Woodard pushed back, stating Durham County, DPS, and City officials all advocated for SB 203/HB 231 and that the Senate President Pro Tem's office simply blocked local bills while county staff already hold general-law authority to partner on restricted-use land.
conflicts.resolution: Interim County Attorney Willie Darby was directed to consult the UNC School of Government and DPS counsel to confirm whether existing statute enables restricted-use conveyance without special legislation.

conflicts.issue: School Board Public Criticism of BOCC Over Teacher Pay ($5,000 Raises) and Affordable Housing
conflicts.summary: Commissioner Nimasheena Burns and Chair Brenda A. Howerton rebuked public statements by School Board members blaming the BOCC for blocking teacher affordable housing and $5,000 pay raises without ever contacting commissioners.
conflicts.side_a_position: Demand direct inter-board communication and condemn public misrepresentations blaming the five women commissioners for stalling housing and teacher supplements.
side_a_arguments: Commissioner Nimasheena Burns noted she received zero direct outreach prior to weekend remarks claiming School Board members had lobbied all five commissioners on affordable housing and teacher raises.
Chair Brenda A. Howerton stated BOCC has not refused teacher housing or youth support and called for the boards to communicate directly rather than assign blame publicly.
conflicts.side_b_position: Note earlier multi-year history underlying the School Board's perspective while continuing legal review of surplus property conveyance.
side_b_arguments: Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs noted the School Board chair referenced earlier historical conversations predating newer members while Interim Attorney Willie Darby awaited a legal mechanism from DPS counsel.
conflicts.resolution: No formal action; commissioners requested that elected peers cease public finger-pointing and engage the Board directly alongside legal staff.

conflicts.issue: Property Tax Reappraisal Schedule: Immediate Commitment to 2025 vs. Waiting for 2022 State Data Under Current 2026 Plan
conflicts.summary: Following Tax Administration's report that Q1 2021 sales ratios dropped to 79.6% (below the 85% statutory trigger) while Farragut software conversion remained on schedule, commissioners disagreed on whether to move toward formally scheduling a 2025 reappraisal now or await state Department of Revenue confirmation under the February 2021 compromise delaying to 2026.
conflicts.side_a_position: Prepare and consider formally scheduling a 2025 general reappraisal rather than waiting until 2026–2027, minimizing cumulative homeowner sticker shock and maintaining shorter assessment cycles.
side_a_arguments: Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs warned a seven-year gap before 2026–2027 exposes homeowners to severe property tax jumps even under a revenue-neutral rate, while shorter 3- to 4-year cycles improve equity.
Commissioner Heidi Carter welcomed Tax Administration's readiness to conduct a 2025 reappraisal ahead of the earlier 2026 schedule.
conflicts.side_b_position: Respect the February 2021 compromise setting 2026 and avoid changing the board's reappraisal date repeatedly until February 2022 trends and April 2022 NCDOR notice clarify whether advancement to 2025 is legally mandated.
side_b_arguments: Commissioner Nimasheena Burns urged colleagues not to pressure Tax Administrator Dwane Brinson again after the board already compromised from 2027 down to 2026 in February.
Interim Manager Claudia Hager recommended returning in February 2022 with additional sales-ratio data and software conversion progress rather than revising the formal schedule prematurely.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote was taken at the work session; Chair Howerton and commissioners agreed to await Tax Administration's February 2022 follow-up update and April 2022 NCDOR statutory notice.

conflicts.issue: Board Training Consultant Selection Process and Open vs. Closed Session Venue
conflicts.summary: Commissioners disagreed over whether discussions of board training consultants and prior RFP policy handling should occur in open or closed session, as well as the propriety of using open-ended commissioner comments for unscheduled policy topics.
conflicts.side_a_position: Discuss RFP policy context and consultant options openly in public session since no statutory closed-session exception applies to board training, and use commissioner comments to inform the public.
side_a_arguments: County legal guidance indicated there is no North Carolina statutory exception allowing closed session for board training.
Publicly clarifying section 5 of the RFP policy prevents half-truths about prior consultant outreach.
conflicts.side_b_position: Keep sensitive personnel/consultant commentary in closed session where appropriate, avoid using open-ended comments as unscheduled agenda items, and establish a formal scope of work for an attorney-led RFP.
side_b_arguments: Open-ended commissioner comment placeholders risk turning unscheduled remarks into de facto agenda items.
Consultant and legal discussions tied to agenda items are more appropriately handled in closed session or through a formal scope-of-work RFP process.
conflicts.resolution: Commissioners agreed by informal consensus at 04:43:50 to submit scope-of-work input for board training to Attorney Darby by Friday so an RFP could be issued.

conflicts.meeting_title: Board of County Commissioners - Work Session for Oct. 7, 2024
conflicts.issue: Capital Improvement Plan (CIP) Prioritization Criteria and Surplus Property Strategy
conflicts.summary: Commissioners challenged staff to establish objective prioritization criteria for the $2B+ CIP pipeline and to reconsider major property commitments like the Boys and Girls Club and old DSS building.
conflicts.side_a_position: Urged an objective, facility-condition-driven priority list, coordinated city-county-DPS infrastructure planning, and re-evaluating Boys and Girls Club and surplus parcels.
side_a_arguments: Urgent aging-infrastructure repairs (mold, leaks) should rank ahead of individual commissioner pet projects.
Land use rezonings drive EMS, sewer, and school capital demands and must be coordinated via a tripartite infrastructure committee.
Selling or repurposing former school sites, surplus downtown lots, and rethinking the Boys and Girls Club site could relieve CIP debt pressures.
conflicts.side_b_position: Staff noted that many CIP projects have been queued for decades and emphasized balancing capital construction with ongoing operating costs and staff capacity.
side_b_arguments: Staff capacity and Durham's AAA bond rating constrain how quickly projects can be delivered.
Worst-case placeholders (like $15M for the old DSS building and $18M for homeless infrastructure) are needed while public-private options are explored.
conflicts.resolution: Staff agreed to send a prioritization feedback template and return in November with refined sequencing, Gant timelines, and affordability scenarios.

conflicts.meeting_title: Board of County Commissioners - FY 2024-25 Budget Work Session #4 - Wednesday, June 4, 2024
conflicts.issue: Scheduling Non-Budget Zafiqo Temple Presentation During Budget Work Session
conflicts.summary: Commissioner Brenda A. Howerton sought to schedule a future September presentation on a Zafiqo Temple land deal at the close of the final budget work session, prompting pushback that non-budget items were inappropriate in the current financial climate and budget session.
conflicts.side_a_position: Place the Zafiqo Temple land deal community presentation on a September agenda
side_a_arguments: Community members undertaking the land deal between Raleigh and Durham requested an opportunity to present to the Board.
conflicts.side_b_position: Defer non-budget presentation requests out of the budget work session to board leadership
side_b_arguments: A presentation involving a land deal is unrelated to the FY 2024-25 budget and inappropriate given the tight financial climate.
