meetings.title: BOCC Work Session for October 3, 2022
meetings.executive_summary: During the October 3, 2022 work session, all five commissioners heard from five public speakers representing Emancipate NC and Tribe NC regarding their report recommending county-level child welfare reforms at Durham County DSS and in dependency courtrooms to reduce involuntary family separations and institutional placements. Following consent agenda review, commissioners discussed DSS family support infrastructure needs and voted 5-0 to suspend work session rules and approve the county's legislative priorities for submission to the North Carolina Association of County Commissioners (NCACC) ahead of a Friday deadline. Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs and Chair Brenda A. Howerton also reported on Regional Transportation Alliance (RTA) Transit Awareness Day—noting rebounding GoTriangle ridership, RDU Airport BRT plans, and county transit grant applications—and Chair Howerton shared procurement and management takeaways from a San Diego conference before a closed personnel session.

agenda_items.title: Citizens' Comments: Emancipate NC and Tribe NC DSS Child Welfare Reform Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Five speakers led by Elizabeth Simpson of Emancipate NC and Tribe NC presented a detailed report based on interviews with foster parents, attorneys, social workers, and Guardian ad Litem volunteers calling for Durham County DSS reforms. Speakers emphasized trauma from involuntary family separation, disproportionate congregate institutional placements for Black youth, and investing resources in biological families and meaningful family time.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Review (17 Items)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The county manager began walking commissioners through 17 consent agenda items starting with item 22-0506, budget ordinance amendment 23BCC0030 recognizing $398,000+ in grant funding.

agenda_items.title: DSS Family Support Needs and Approval of NCACC Legislative Goals Submission
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Concluding the DSS discussion, officials noted Durham County DSS supports family-preservation goals but needs local provider infrastructure and state/federal funding to implement new plans. Because the list was due to the NC Association of County Commissioners (NCACC) by Friday, the board voted 5-0 to suspend the rules and 5-0 to approve submitting its legislative items.

agenda_items.title: Commissioner Conference Reports: RTA Transit Awareness Day and San Diego Conference
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Vice Chair Jacobs and Chair Howerton reported on the Regional Transportation Alliance's inaugural Transit Awareness Day tour across RTP, Triangle Regional Transit Center, and Raleigh Union Station, highlighting GoTriangle's steady all-day bus ridership recovery, RDU Airport's Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) planning, commuter rail alternatives, and Transportation Manager Ellen Beckman's presentation on a county transit grant application. Chair Howerton also shared procurement cost-saving strategies and an employee-focused book from her San Diego conference.

agenda_items.title: Closed Session (Personnel)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The board voted 5-0 to enter closed session under G.S. 143-318.11(a)(6) for personnel/public officer employment matters. Returning at 05:36:30, the board gave direction to staff with no action taken.

votes.item_title: Suspend Work Session Rules for NCACC Legislative Goals Submission
votes.discussion_detail: Board suspended rules to vote on legislative goal submissions due to NCACC by Friday.

votes.item_title: Approve Submission of County Legislative Items to NCACC
votes.discussion_detail: Approved the finalized list of county legislative proposals for submission to the NC Association of County Commissioners after minor wording adjustments.

votes.item_title: Motion to Enter Closed Session (G.S. 143-318.11(a)(6))
votes.notes: Returned at 05:36:30 with no formal action taken.
votes.discussion_detail: Board adjourned to closed session on personnel matters.

meetings.title: BOCC - September 28, 2022 - Regular Session
meetings.executive_summary: Rescheduled to Wednesday evening September 28, 2022 due to religious holidays, the Durham Board of County Commissioners met with all five members present under Chair Brenda A. Howerton. The board approved the September 6 and September 12 minutes, recognized departing Chief of Staff Drew Cummings for 14 years of service, issued proclamations for Cybersecurity Awareness Month and Minority Enterprise Development (MED) Week, and welcomed the county's new Immigrant and Refugee Community Coordinator. Commissioners also highlighted a USDA urban agriculture feasibility grant for the farm campus (item 22-0546), received an annual economic impact update from the Durham Sports Commission ($10.4 million across 34 events), and heard a Public Health report noting Durham's transition to low COVID-19 transmission alongside leading statewide monkeypox vaccination totals before entering a closed session on economic development incentives.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Announcements, and Approval of Minutes (September 6 and September 12, 2022)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Howerton opened the rescheduled Wednesday session, read the public charge, and noted Suicide Prevention Awareness Month statistics showing an 11% rise in firearm suicides between 2014 and 2020 alongside clerk announcements for COVID-19 clinics and Sheriff Birkhead's October 5 Coffee with a Cop. Commissioners unanimously approved the September 6 work session and September 12 regular session minutes.

agenda_items.title: Farewell Tribute to Drew Cummings and Ceremonial Proclamations (Cybersecurity Month, MED Week, and Immigrant/Refugee Coordinator)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Commissioners thanked Drew Cummings for 14 years of county service. The board then presented proclamations for Cybersecurity Awareness Month (highlighting NIST frameworks and Durham's 2017 Information Security Program) and Minority Enterprise Development (MED) Week (October 3-7, 2022, read by Commissioner Burns and citing Durham's M/WBE ordinance and pandemic disparities), and welcomed the county's new Immigrant and Refugee Community Coordinator.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Review (Including Item 22-0546 USDA Farm Campus Feasibility Grant)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The board reviewed six consent items (22-0486, 22-0546, 22-0553, 22-0557, 22-0558, and 22-0591). Without pulling item 22-0546, commissioners asked staff member Donna to briefly describe the USDA urban agriculture feasibility grant awarded for the county's farm campus; the subsequent vote sequence lies within a truncated portion of the transcript digest.

agenda_items.title: Durham Sports Commission Annual Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Durham Sports Commission Executive Director Marcus Manning reported that the commission supported 34 events generating over $10.4 million in economic impact and 16,000 hotel room nights, hosted Durham's first NAIA national championship and the Champion Durham Classic high school basketball invitational, and awaited a November 12 site vote between Durham and South Korea. Manning also discussed scouting land for a youth/regional sports complex and potential Memorial Stadium projects, while commissioners raised questions on sponsorship, local youth access, and land availability.

agenda_items.title: Public Health Update: COVID-19 Transmission and Monkeypox Response
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Health Director Rod Jenkins reported that Durham County had moved into the CDC 'green' (low transmission) category, thanked commissioners for supporting a second wastewater surveillance site, and urged flu vaccination ahead of an anticipated severe flu season. Jenkins also reported 38 identified monkeypox cases in Durham (100% male and 73.68% Black/African American) and nearly 800 vaccinations administered, ranking first in North Carolina.

agenda_items.title: Commissioner Comments and Closed Session (Economic Development Incentives)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: A commissioner recognized community figure Linda from Saturday's Pride march before the board voted 5-0 to enter closed session under G.S. 143-318.11(a)(4) to discuss business location or expansion and tentative economic development incentives. The board returned and adjourned at 04:08:02.

meetings.title: BOCC - September 12, 2022 - Regular Session
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over the September 12, 2022 Durham Board of County Commissioners Regular Session with all five commissioners present following Commissioner Nida Allam's return from maternity leave. The Board unanimously approved meeting minutes, the consent agenda (excluding pulled item 22-0508), and ceremonial proclamations for National Recovery Month, Operation Green Light for Veterans, and World Alzheimer's and Dementia Awareness Day. Following a lengthy quasi-judicial hearing and board debate over whether to continue the case for neighbor expert review after a notice URL error, the Board voted 5-0 to approve Mason Farms Major Special Use Permit M220001 and Major Site Plan D2100325 for a 141-lot conservation subdivision served by private community wells and drip-irrigation wastewater systems. The Board also referred item 22-0540 back to staff due to a notification defect, unanimously approved renaming Park Drive to Sankar Way (SN22001), and voted 5-0 to approve the City-County Interlocal Agreement for DSS administration of the Low-Income Homeowners Relief Program (22-0508) after contentious public comment over CPS practices led to a speaker's removal.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Pledge of Allegiance, Public Charge, and Community Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton called the meeting to order, Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs led the Pledge of Allegiance, and Chair Howerton read the public charge. Clerk announcements highlighted COVID-19 and pediatric vaccination clinics, Low-Income Homeowners Relief (LIHR) outreach, the Food Security Network meeting, a Women's Health Conference, Vietnam Veterans memorial activities, and the Safe School Summit, alongside a moment of silence for 9/11 and the passing of former County Attorney Lowell Siler. Commissioner Nida Allam joined the dais at 00:35:53.

agenda_items.title: Approval of August 2022 Meeting Minutes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presented the minutes from the August 11 work session and the August 8 and August 22, 2022 regular sessions. No corrections or edits were requested by the commissioners.

agenda_items.title: Ceremonial Proclamations: National Recovery Month (22-0515), Operation Green Light (22-0516), and World Alzheimer's Day (22-0561)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Commissioner Heidi Carter read proclamation 22-0515 recognizing September as National Recovery Month, joined by Recovery Community of Durham leader Michelle McKinney and Board Chair Larry McGill. Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs read proclamation 22-0516 endorsing Operation Green Light for Veterans (November 7-13), and Commissioner Nimasheena Burns read proclamation 22-0561 designating September 21 as World Alzheimer's and Dementia Awareness Day, with remarks from Susan Sewell of Dementia Inclusive Inc.

agenda_items.title: Approval of Consent Agenda (Excluding Pulled Item 22-0508)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The Board pulled item 22-0508 for public comment and voted unanimously to approve the remainder of the consent agenda, which included the FY22-23 Bull City Community Schools contract with the DPS Foundation (22-0440), Whispering Pines stormwater ARPA grant resolution (22-0479), $20,000 NC DHHS tobacco-free grant (22-0492), Justice Assistance Grant review (22-0493), a $158,866 InTelecom Detention Center AV/telecom contract (22-0509), and Board of Elections temporary staffing (22-0510). Following the vote, Commissioner Burns highlighted the approval of $5.2 million in 2016 bond funds for the newly named Murray-Massenburg Elementary School.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing 22-0539: Mason Farms Major Special Use Permit (M220001) and Major Site Plan (D2100325)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Cole Renninger and Planning Director Sara Young presented Triple I Capital Management's quasi-judicial applications for a 287.723-acre conservation subdivision (141 single-family lots, >50% open space, <=6% impervious surface) off Preston Andrews Road served by private community wells and a subsurface drip-irrigation wastewater treatment system. Applicant attorney Patrick Byker and four expert witnesses testified that all Unified Development Ordinance review factors were met, while neighboring residents Catherine Ross, Thomas Freeman, and Pamela Andrews urged postponement because of a wrong City URL on the hearing notice and unfamiliarity with quasi-judicial expert rules. After closing the hearing and debating a 30-to-60-day continuance versus deciding on the completed record, the Board approved both M220001 and D2100325 unanimously.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 5-0 (Hearing opened 5-0; M220001 approved 5-0; D2100325 approved 5-0)

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing 22-0540: Partial Closing of Akron Boulevard
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented item 22-0540 concerning the proposed closing of a 970-linear-foot portion of Akron Boulevard removed from the NCDOT secondary road maintenance system. Staff recommended pulling the item from the agenda and referring it back to staff due to a public notification defect.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Pulled / Referred back to staff (No vote)

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing 22-0541: Street Renaming Case SN22001 (Park Drive to Sankar Way)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented the Research Triangle Foundation's request under G.S. 153A-239.1 to rename Park Drive, a private business park street affecting three constructed buildings, to Sankar Way. The Board voted 5-0 to open the public hearing, heard no speakers, and voted 5-0 to approve SN22001.

agenda_items.title: Other Business 22-0543 (Removed) and Pulled Consent Item 22-0508: Low-Income Homeowners Relief Program Interlocal Agreement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Howerton announced item 22-0543 was removed for a future agenda, then took up pulled consent item 22-0508 establishing a City-County Interlocal Agreement for DSS to administer the Low-Income Homeowners Relief (LIHR) Program. Speakers Amanda Wallace and Lee Smith opposed DSS administering the program over Child Protective Services grievances, and Chair Howerton had a deputy escort Smith out for speaking off-topic after refusing to stop. Commissioner Burns and staff clarified that the updated LIHR program lowered residency requirements from 10 to 5 years and provides grants up to 50% of property taxes ($1,000 to $1,500 by AMI tier) before the Board approved the ILA 5-0.

votes.item_title: Approval of August 11 Work Session and August 8 & August 22, 2022 Regular Session Minutes
votes.notes: Unanimous roll-call approval following Nida Allam's return to the Board.
votes.discussion_detail: No additions or corrections were proposed for the August 11 work session and August 8 and 22 regular session minutes, and the motion passed unanimously by roll call.

votes.item_title: Approval of Consent Agenda (Excluding Pulled Item 22-0508)
votes.notes: Item 22-0508 (City-County LIHR Interlocal Agreement) was pulled for public comment and voted on separately at the end of the meeting.
votes.discussion_detail: Upon request to pull item 22-0508 for citizen speakers, the Board moved, seconded, and unanimously approved all remaining consent items, including grant recognitions, school capital funding transfers, Detention Center telecom/AV contracts, and Board of Elections temporary staffing.

votes.item_title: Open Quasi-Judicial Public Hearing for Item 22-0539 (Mason Farms M220001 and D2100325)
votes.notes: Followed staff presentation and pre-hearing clarifying questions from commissioners; witnesses were then sworn in.
votes.discussion_detail: Before taking sworn testimony from applicant experts and neighboring property owners on the Mason Farms community wastewater system and site plan, the Board voted unanimously by roll call to open the quasi-judicial public hearing.

votes.item_title: Approve Major Special Use Permit M220001 (Mason Farms Community Wastewater System, Item 22-0539)
votes.notes: Nimasheena Burns noted while voting aye that staff must address communication/notice issues going forward ('y'all got to tighten up').
votes.discussion_detail: After extensive testimony from four applicant expert witnesses and three neighboring residents requesting a postponement due to a broken URL on the mailed notice, the Board debated whether a continuance was legally justified. Concluding that competent, material, and substantial expert evidence established compliance with all 13 UDO review factors and general findings, Commissioner Heidi Carter moved to approve M220001, which passed 5-0 by roll call.

votes.item_title: Approve Major Site Plan D2100325 (Mason Farms Conservation Subdivision, Item 22-0539)
votes.notes: Associated by-right conservation subdivision major site plan contingent on MSUP M220001 approval.
votes.discussion_detail: Following approval of Major Special Use Permit M220001, a commissioner moved approval of Major Site Plan D2100325 as a by-right development meeting all Unified Development Ordinance requirements, which passed 5-0 by roll call.

votes.item_title: Open Public Hearing for Item 22-0541 (Street Renaming SN22001: Park Drive to Sankar Way)
votes.notes: Private street renaming requested by Research Triangle Foundation.
votes.discussion_detail: Following staff's brief summary confirming statutory compliance under G.S. 153A-239.1 and zero agency objections, the Board unanimously opened the public hearing on street renaming case SN22001.

votes.item_title: Approve Street Renaming Case SN22001 (Park Drive to Sankar Way, Item 22-0541)
votes.notes: No speakers appeared during the public hearing.
votes.discussion_detail: With no members of the public signed up to speak, Chair Howerton closed the hearing and the Board voted 5-0 by roll call to rename Park Drive to Sankar Way.

votes.item_title: Approve Pulled Consent Item 22-0508 (City-County ILA for DSS Administration of Low-Income Homeowners Relief Program)
votes.notes: Pulled for public speakers criticizing DSS/CPS; Commissioner Burns and DSS staff clarified updated 5-year residency and tiered grant rules prior to the vote.
votes.discussion_detail: After public comments criticizing DSS over child welfare cases—including the removal of speaker Lee Smith for off-topic remarks—Commissioner Nimasheena Burns and DSS staff outlined the expanded Low-Income Homeowners Relief program tiers ($1,000 to $1,500 up to 50% of property taxes, reduced 5-year residency requirement). The Board then approved the City-County interlocal agreement 5-0 by roll call.

disagreements.issue: Continuance vs. Immediate Quasi-Judicial Decision on Mason Farms Community Wastewater Permit (M220001)
disagreements.summary: Following neighbor testimony protesting a broken City website link on the mailed public notice and unfamiliarity with quasi-judicial expert-witness rules, Chair Brenda A. Howerton read an attorney-prepared draft continuance to November 14, 2022, triggering board debate over whether continuing the hearing was legally appropriate or fair to all parties.
disagreements.side_a_position: Continue the quasi-judicial hearing (for 30 to 60 days) to allow neighboring residents time to review documents and retain experts given notice confusion.
side_a_arguments: The mailed notice letter directed residents to an incorrect City URL, creating barriers to accessing staff materials prior to the hearing.
Neighbors unfamiliar with quasi-judicial evidentiary rules requested additional time to consult wastewater and hydrology experts.
disagreements.side_b_position: Proceed to vote immediately on the closed evidentiary record because all legal notice requirements and UDO review factors were satisfied.
side_b_arguments: Planning Director Sara Young confirmed the broken URL was not a statutory or UDO notice defect, and the applicant already held an extended hearing with sworn experts.
Under quasi-judicial law, if competent, substantial evidence meets every UDO standard and no rebuttal expert evidence exists, the Board cannot deny or delay merely out of neighborhood opposition.
disagreements.resolution: After legal counsel advised putting a motion on the floor to vote up or down, Commissioner Carter moved approval of M220001, Commissioner Jacobs came around to the UDO standard, and the Board voted 5-0 to approve both M220001 and D2100325 without a continuance.

meetings.title: BOCC Work Session for September 6, 2022
meetings.executive_summary: Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs opened the September 6, 2022 BOCC Work Session before Chair Brenda A. Howerton assumed the chair, with Commissioner Nida Allam absent on maternity leave (four commissioners present). Commissioners reviewed September 12 consent agenda items, heard comprehensive policy briefings on the 18-year North Carolina Opioid Litigation Settlement framework (22-0524) and the Management Advisory Group classification and compensation study (13 public-sector peers plus O*NET data), and engaged in pointed debate over GoTriangle's draft Greater Triangle Commuter Rail Feasibility Study showing costs rising 50% to $2.8B-$3.2B and questioning phased corridors and federal New Starts viability. The Board also received updates on $62.4 million in ARPA spending and Phase 1 community grants (22-0390/ARPA) and Durham's $1.7 million FY22 Food Security Initiative, unanimously suspended the rules (4-0) to adopt Durham's 2023 NCACC Legislative Goals (22-0529), and held the first required public hearing on a $950,000 CDBG Neighborhood Revitalization grant application.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Public Charge, and Consent Agenda Review
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs called the work session to order at 9:10 AM with no citizen commenters present, and County Manager Kimberly Sowell walked commissioners through 22 consent items for September 12, including Whispering Pines ARPA stormwater planning (22-0478, $500,000), LIHR ILA (22-0508), Governor's Highway Safety Program grant (22-0514), Master Aging Plan ILA (22-0518), Stanford L. Warren Library interior design amendment (22-0519, $105,240), sanitary sewer extensions (22-0523), Murray-Massenburg Elementary bond transfer (22-0528, $5.20M), Kirstie Fontaine LLC equity contract (22-0530, $101,400), Westaff and Cure Violence Global contracts for Bull City United (22-0531, 22-0532), and Cates' Corner student learning center (22-0534). Commissioners pressed staff on sewer capacity under the 1972 City-County agreement, adding gender identity/expression clauses to contracts, and Bull City United temporary-to-permanent hiring.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0524: Proposed Framework for Acceptance and Distribution of Opioid Litigation Settlement Proceeds
agenda_items.discussion_summary: NCACC Director Nidhi Shashtaveda and Interim General Manager Gudrun Palmer outlined North Carolina's $750M+ 18-year opioid settlement framework—including Durham County's front-loaded payments (~$450,000 initial balance settling to ~$511,000 annually through 2038)—comparing Option A's 12 vetted high-impact strategies with Option B. Staff inventoried local efforts such as Detention Center Phase 2 MOUD induction, Community Paramedics, Lincoln Community Health Center, and Durham Joins Together. Board consensus directed staff to deploy a community survey prior to public town halls, build a public webpage inventorying existing resources, eliminate co-pay barriers at Lincoln, prioritize equity, and require funded housing/employment providers to allow low-barrier MOUD access.

agenda_items.title: Classification and Compensation Study Update (Management Advisory Group International)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: MAG Senior Vice President Dr. Russell Campbell detailed the countywide classification and compensation study methodology, including 14 job evaluation factors, online employee questionnaires (Sept 20-Oct 3), supervisor reviews (Oct 4-11), O*NET private-sector data, addressing salary compression, and targeting three separate pay plans with a draft report before Thanksgiving. Commissioners endorsed expanding the survey peer list from 10 to 13 jurisdictions by adding Wake, Guilford, and Charlotte-Mecklenburg counties, and Commissioner Heidi Carter urged structuring the forthcoming compensation philosophy to ensure a living wage even where market rates fall short.

agenda_items.title: Greater Triangle Commuter Rail Feasibility Study Update (GoTriangle)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Transportation Manager Ellen Beckman, GoTriangle CEO Chuck Lattuca, and Chief Development Officer Katharine Eggleston presented draft Phase 2 findings showing projected West Durham-to-Garner/Clayton capital costs surged 50% to $2.8B-$3.2B ($42M/year O&M, 12,000-18,000 daily riders by 2040, opening 2033-2035), putting the 50% federal New Starts rating at risk. GoTriangle outlined three possible starter phases—West Durham to RTP ($1.6B), Raleigh to RTP/Ellis Road ($1.0B), and Southeast Wake ($600M)—alongside urgent October IIJA Rail Crossing Elimination grant applications for Plum Street, Driver Street, and Ellis Road. Commissioners sharply challenged any Phase 1 excluding Durham County, raised small Black business impacts on Driver Street, and questioned whether Bus Rapid Transit or local micro-transit alternatives merit comparison alongside the $300M Durham Transit Plan update.

agenda_items.title: American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Deputy County Manager Claudia Hager reported on the $62.4 million ARPA allocation ($5.1M budgeted / $1.9M expended in FY22; $6.8M budgeted in FY23), Frontier's >$2M State GREAT Grant and the county's broadband RFP for 100% northern Durham coverage, and over $230 million in city/county requests competing for roughly $10 million in Phase 1 community grants closed August 15. Staff previewed October policy sessions on Phase 2 grants, joint City-County affordable housing/mental health/youth ILAs, and fund balance capacity building for smaller nonprofits. Commissioners Burns, Jacobs, and Carter debated revising the ARPA framework so Phase 2 targets larger transformative investments—especially permanent affordable housing—rather than small fragmented awards.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0529: Proposed Items for 2023 NCACC Legislative Goals Process
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Deborah Craig-Ray and Assistant County Attorney Curtis Massey reviewed updated 2023 NCACC legislative goals ahead of the September 12 submission deadline, adding Commissioner Burns' proposal to raise the NC high school dropout age from 16 to 18, separating Chair Howerton's childcare funding item (300% FPL), incorporating Vice Chair Jacobs' physical/behavioral health data-sharing edit, consolidating protection for public officials/employees/election workers, adding Commissioner Carter's Extreme Risk Protection Order ('red flag') gun safety language, and proposing G.S. 166A-19.24 remote-meeting authority for public bodies. The Board voted 4-0 to suspend the rules and 4-0 to approve the legislative goals package.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0390: County Food Security Initiative Update and Upcoming Plans
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Cooperative Extension Director Donna Rewalt and Food Security Coordinator Mary Oxendine reported that ~10% of Durham residents experience very low food security (1 in 4 Latinx residents and 1 in 6 Black residents) and summarized FY22's $1.7 million County investment (69% to BIPOC-led organizations, >29,000 households served, 3,500 produce boxes, $400,000 to 26 nonprofits). They outlined FY23 priorities including $475,000 in community grants, a $150,000 comprehensive food system assessment, a cross-departmental City-County-DPS team, and a $167,000 USDA grant to study an incubator Farm Campus, while warning Blue Cross funding for Double Bucks expires at year-end. Commissioners urged addressing senior/immigrant transportation barriers, food waste, and farmworker wages.

agenda_items.title: Follow-Up on Commissioner Directives and First Public Hearing on CDBG Neighborhood Revitalization Grant
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chief of Staff Drew Cummings updated commissioners on pending directives, and Commissioner Carter asked that the single-use plastic bag fee return to the October work session before going to the Joint City-County Committee. Cummings then presented the first of two required public hearings for a $950,000 state CDBG Neighborhood Revitalization grant (backed by a $100,000 local match) to fund home and septic repairs outside Durham city limits through the Durham Home Repair Collaborative ahead of a September 28 second hearing. After opening and closing the public hearing with no speakers, the Board voted 4-0 to suspend the rules for holding a public hearing during a work session.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 4-0 (Rules suspended to hold hearing; Grant resolution deferred to Sept. 28)

votes.item_title: Motion to Suspend the Rules to Vote on 2023 NCACC Legislative Goals During Work Session (Item 22-0529)
votes.notes: Nida Allam absent on maternity leave. Rules suspension required to take binding action at a work session ahead of NCACC's September 12 deadline.
votes.discussion_detail: Because September 12 was the NCACC deadline for submitting 2023 legislative goal proposals and fell before the next regular voting meeting, the Board voted 4-0 by roll call to suspend its rules to adopt the package.

votes.item_title: Approve Proposed Items for 2023 NCACC Legislative Goals Process (Item 22-0529)
votes.notes: Nida Allam absent on maternity leave. Included Leandro funding, high school dropout age 16-to-18 pilot/mandate, standalone childcare funding, remote meeting statutory authority, gun safety/red flag ERPOs, transit, and courts funding.
votes.discussion_detail: Following review of revisions requested at the August 22 meeting—plus new items on the dropout age (16 to 18) and remote public-body meeting clarity—the Board unanimously approved the final 2023 NCACC legislative goals list by a 4-0 roll call.

votes.item_title: Motion to Suspend the Rules to Hold CDBG Neighborhood Revitalization Grant Public Hearing During Work Session
votes.notes: Nida Allam absent on maternity leave. No grant resolution action was taken; second public hearing and formal resolution scheduled for September 28, 2022.
votes.discussion_detail: After Chief of Staff Drew Cummings presented the first required public hearing for a $950,000 state CDBG Neighborhood Revitalization grant (with $100,000 county match) for unincorporated home/septic repairs and no speakers came forward, the Board voted 4-0 by roll call to suspend the rules authorizing the public hearing during a work session.

disagreements.issue: Durham Inclusion in Phase 1 vs. Alternative Investments for the Greater Triangle Commuter Rail Study
disagreements.summary: Following GoTriangle's report that full West Durham-to-Garner/Clayton commuter rail costs jumped 50% to $2.8B-$3.2B, commissioners clashed over GoTriangle's proposed starter-phase options, private-sector/business displacement concerns, and whether commuter rail remains viable compared with Bus Rapid Transit and local micro-transit.
disagreements.side_a_position: Durham County must be included in any Phase 1 corridor with Wake County (not Johnston County first), with aggressive federal IIJA/FRA grant pursuit and private-sector/RTP funding participation.
side_a_arguments: Durham taxpayers passed the half-cent transit sales tax long ago while Johnston County has no dedicated transit tax.
With 2050 traffic maps turning solid red and regional job growth concentrating east of Durham, leaving Durham residents out of Phase 1 would cut them off from economic mobility.
Staff and GoTriangle must pursue 80/20 federal Rail Crossing Elimination grants immediately and bring RTP/business leaders into early co-funding talks.
disagreements.side_b_position: Question high Durham-segment costs ($1.6B), Driver Street small Black business displacement, lack of complete federal funding plans, and whether $3.2B-scale spending would be better directed to BRT and localized rapid transit.
side_b_arguments: Commissioners need a full menu of feasible federal funding pots before committing, as current revenue appears insufficient for a $2.8B-$3.2B build.
East Durham's Driver Street corridor contains roughly seven small Black-owned businesses that could be harmed by host-railroad crossing closures.
Localized micro-transit or Bus Rapid Transit along corridors like 15-501 and West Durham-Ellis Road may serve Durham's near-term needs better than relying on long commuter lines.
disagreements.resolution: Informational discussion concluded without a vote; GoTriangle committed to bring back a federal grant matrix and conduct a 45-day public engagement period, while County staff scheduled a Durham Transit Plan update for October.

meetings.title: BOCC - August 22, 2022 - Regular Session
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over the August 22, 2022 Regular Session with four commissioners present (Commissioner Nida Allam absent on maternity leave). The Board heard an update on the Solarize the Triangle/Durham solar subsidy program, recognized outgoing 20-year System of Care staffer and commissioners' NACo leadership appointments, and jointly read a Resolution in Support of Reproductive Justice and Freedom responding to the Dobbs Supreme Court ruling and reinstatement of North Carolina's 20-week abortion ban. After citizen Antoinette Haas commented on workforce development, Greater Durham Black Chamber funding (22-0464), and Engineering due diligence funds (22-0489), the Board voted 4-0 to approve the consent agenda excluding pulled items 22-0485 and 22-0487, which passed 4-0 separately after a Kids Voting / 4-H Cooperative Extension presentation. Commissioners also received Public Health Director Rod Jenkins' COVID-19 and monkeypox briefing (flagging vaccine disparities among Black residents), reviewed draft 2023 NCACC legislative goals (22-0494) while deferring formal adoption to September, and announced appointments to seven boards and commissions.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Solarize Durham Update, Staff Tribute, and NACo Recognitions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton opened the meeting and Sustainability Manager Tobin Freed reported on the Solarize the Triangle campaign, noting Durham City and County each contributed $50,000 toward low-income solar installations boosted by the 30% federal Inflation Reduction Act tax credit. The Board also recognized retiring 20-year Family Partner Coordinator Tika for System of Care leadership and acknowledged NACo committee vice-chair and network appointments for Commissioners Burns and Jacobs.

agenda_items.title: Ceremonial Resolution in Support of Reproductive Justice and Freedom
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Commissioners Heidi Carter, Nimasheena Burns, Wendy Jacobs, and Chair Brenda A. Howerton jointly read a ceremonial resolution affirming bodily autonomy, expanding Durham County Public Health reproductive/family planning access, and directing staff to identify local actions protecting abortion and reproductive care access following the Supreme Court's Dobbs decision and federal court reinstatement of North Carolina's 20-week ban. Burns also credited absent Commissioner Nida Allam for background work and delivered prepared remarks linking reproductive rights to maternal health investments.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Ceremonial reading / No formal roll-call vote

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Approval and Pulled Kids Voting Items (22-0485, 22-0487) & Tax Settlement Review (22-0491)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Citizen Antoinette Haas spoke on workforce development item 22-0461 ($250,000), argued $50,000 for the Greater Durham Black Chamber of Commerce (22-0464) was too small, and criticized $150,000 for Engineering legal/due diligence costs (22-0489). After pulling items 22-0485 and 22-0487 for Cooperative Extension briefing, the Board passed the remainder of the consent agenda 4-0. Cooperative Extension Director Donna Rewalt and Kids Voting Coordinator Carolyn Krueger highlighted statewide 4-H and Orange County partnerships before the Board approved 22-0485 and 22-0487 by 4-0 vote, followed by Tax Administrator Dwayne Brenson explaining North Carolina's 10-year tax collection statute of limitations on item 22-0491.

agenda_items.title: Durham County Public Health Focus Update (COVID-19 and Monkeypox)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Health Director Rod Jenkins reported 702 new COVID-19 cases over seven days, four additional deaths, 88.9% BA.5 variant prevalence, ~200 daily at-home test distributions, and 1,500 pre-ordered Moderna/Pfizer autumn boosters. Jenkins also highlighted 19 confirmed monkeypox cases in Durham County—100% male and 78.58% Black/African American—urging Black residents to utilize free, discreet JYNNEOS vaccinations as the department transitioned to intradermal dosing.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0494: Review of Proposed 2023 NCACC Legislative Goals
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Deborah Craig-Ray led the Board through updated draft NCACC legislative goals ahead of the September 12 submission deadline, covering Leandro school funding, community college support (Allam), standalone childcare/women-and-children funding and nursing home oversight (Howerton), Familiar Faces data sharing and homestead circuit-breaker/transit goals (Jacobs), economic development and workforce housing (Burns), an $18.50 living wage and youth gun safety laws (Carter), broadband preemption (Allam), and protections for election workers/public officials alongside increased NC courts funding. Commissioners agreed to defer formal voting until the September 6 work session to allow final edits.

agenda_items.title: Boards and Commissions Appointments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Interim County Attorney Willie Darby announced the Board's ballot appointments across seven bodies: Demetrius Smith (Boxing and Wrestling Commission), Miran (Criminal Justice Advisory Committee), Andrew Nurkin (Durham Cultural Advisory Board), Brandon Davis (Planning Commission), Nisha Williams (Durham Racial Equity Commission), Russell Pierce (Homeless Services Advisory Committee), and Milan McMillan, Ida Stringer-Standback, Miguel Jackson, and Willis Richard (Library Board). meetings.title: BOCC - August 8, 2022 - Regular Session
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over the August 8, 2022 Regular Session with all five commissioners present—Commissioner Nida Allam's final meeting before maternity leave. The Board approved June 27 and July 11 minutes 5-0, honored retiring Duke Regional Hospital President Katie Galbraith, proclaimed Child Support Awareness Month ($15.95M collected in FY21-22), and read a statement on Durham County's new Non-Discrimination Ordinance effective July 1. Commissioners approved the main consent agenda 5-0 and then addressed five pulled items (22-0439, 22-0447, 22-0470, 22-0476, and 22-0477), hearing sharp public criticism of DSS/CPS child welfare funding alongside strong support for three major County real estate acquisitions: $6 million to buy the former John Avery Boys & Girls Club for Bull City United/CISS, $12.15 million net to acquire the 17-acre Shops at Hope Valley (including a former Kroger) for a consolidated 54,000-square-foot Board of Elections facility, and an adjacent 3+ acre Bram Office Supply parcel for Durham Tech expansion; all five pulled items passed 5-0.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Pledge, Announcements, and Approval of Minutes (June 27 and July 11, 2022)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton called the meeting to order, Commissioner Nimasheena Burns led the Pledge of Allegiance, and clerk announcements highlighted COVID-19 testing/vaccines, Sheriff Speaks on eviction prevention, Pre-K, the Transit Plan survey, August 15 ARPA deadlines, LIHR applications, and the 'I Voted' sticker contest. The Board then approved the June 27 and July 11, 2022 meeting minutes 5-0.

agenda_items.title: Ceremonial Recognitions and Non-Discrimination Ordinance Statement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Commissioners presented a Resolution of Appreciation honoring retiring Duke Regional Hospital President & CEO Katie B. Galbraith for her partnership during the pandemic. Commissioner Heidi Carter read the Child Support Awareness Month 2022 proclamation with DSS Director Ben Rose ($15,946,090.39 collected in FY21-22 for 8,373 children), and Chair Howerton read a statement marking the July 1 effective date of Durham County's Non-Discrimination Ordinance in unincorporated areas.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Batch 1 (Excluding Five Pulled Items)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Five items (22-0439, 22-0447, 22-0470, 22-0476, and 22-0477) were pulled for public comment and staff presentations, and the Board approved all remaining consent items 5-0 by roll call. Following the vote, Commissioner Burns announced the third Stanford L. Warren Library community input session set for August 17.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Items (22-0439, 22-0447, 22-0470, 22-0476, and 22-0477): DSS Grants and Strategic County Real Estate Purchases
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Speakers Kiki Woods, Alexis Nguyen, Kelly Smith, and Antoinette Haas opposed DSS receiving $33,000 in Chafee/LINKS foster-youth funds (22-0439) and $878,457 in aging Home & Community Care Block Grant funds (22-0447) over CPS removal allegations, while Commissioner Burns clarified the latter is federal aging daycare funding. Staff and agency leaders (Joanne Pierce, Perry Manns, Nancy Mitchell, Elections Director Derek Bowens, and Durham Tech President J.B. Buxton) then detailed three strategic acquisitions: $6M LOBs financing to buy the former John Avery Boys & Girls Club for Bull City United/CISS (22-0470), $12,146,717 net ($14M minus repair credits) for the 17-acre Shops at Hope Valley to house a consolidated 54,000-sq-ft Board of Elections center and early voting site while honoring 24 existing tenant leases pending public engagement (22-0476), and the 3+ acre Bram warehouse adjacent to Durham Tech (22-0477); all five items passed 5-0.

agenda_items.title: Closing Commissioner Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Commissioner Nida Allam announced that Durham County Public Health was scheduling monkeypox vaccinations for high-risk residents and noted this was her final meeting before departing on maternity leave, after which the Board adjourned 5-0.

meetings.title: BOCC Work Session for August 1, 2022, Part 2
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over the August 1, 2022 Part 2 Work Session, beginning mid-briefing on Durham's draft Comprehensive Plan before turning to the City-County HEART pilot interlocal agreement, 2023 NCACC legislative goal proposals, NCACC voting delegate selection, commissioner directives, and a closed session. Staff outlined the HEART pilot's deployment of three City-funded County EMT-Basics alongside Crisis Call Diversion, 3-person Community Response Teams, and Care Navigation with zero safety backup incidents in its first month. Commissioners voted 5-0 to suspend the rules and appoint Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs as NCACC voting delegate and Commissioner Nimasheena Burns as alternate. Following a closed session under G.S. 143-318.11(a)(5) (with four commissioners present, Nida Allam absent), the Board voted 4-0 to authorize staff to submit a $100,000 opening bid for a county real property purchase and respond to any upset bids.

agenda_items.title: Draft New Comprehensive Plan Briefing and Feedback
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff continued presenting the draft Durham Comprehensive Plan (incorporating an Urban Growth Boundary retracted by 13 square miles relative to 2005 tiers, Future Growth Areas, 20 place types, and 227 policies to accommodate 130,000 new residents and 60,000 housing units by 2050). Commissioners Burns, Jacobs, Carter, and Howerton pushed for expanded rural outreach (including Bahama), large printed maps, clearer Urban Growth Boundary enforceability, public-land priorities, and equitable 15-minute neighborhood infrastructure before breaking for lunch at 00:46:31.

agenda_items.title: City-County Interlocal Agreement for EMT Support of Community Safety Department's HEART Pilot
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Durham Community Safety Director Ryan Smith, Deputy City Manager Bo Ferguson, Clinical Manager Abena Bediako, Assistant Director Aniese Vance, and EMS Chief Mark Lockhart presented the one-year HEART pilot (Crisis Call Diversion in 911, 3-person unarmed Community Response Teams pairing clinicians, peers, and City-funded County EMT-Basics, Care Navigation follow-up, and Co-Response), reporting zero safety or law enforcement backup incidents during its first month of operation. All five commissioners questioned dispatch scripts, clinician retention, shared clinical data platforms, co-responder de-escalation, and scaling non-police response countywide.

agenda_items.title: Initial Solicitation of 2023 NCACC Legislative Goals
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Deborah Craig-Ray and department heads Jim Groves (Emergency Management), Ben Rose (DSS), Curtis Massey (County Attorney's Office), and Rod Jenkins (Public Health) presented staff proposals—including emergency-management insurance-fee funding, Medicaid expansion/50% state child-welfare cost share, remote-meeting authority under locally declared emergencies, lower lead-hazard thresholds, prenatal care access, and a flagged conflict over social-worker title protection—alongside commissioner priorities on Leandro funding, transit, workforce housing, living wage, gun safety, community colleges, broadband preemption, and election-worker safety. Commissioners deferred formal adoption to a later session.

agenda_items.title: NCACC 115th Annual Conference Voting Delegates and Commissioner Comments/Directives
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The Board voted 5-0 to suspend its rules and 5-0 to appoint Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs as voting delegate and Commissioner Nimasheena Burns as alternate for the NCACC 115th Annual Conference. Chair Howerton announced her appointment to the NACo Board of Directors, Vice Chair Jacobs highlighted 988 behavioral-health call data and Familiar Faces data-sharing models from Johnson County, Kansas, Commissioner Carter flagged the pending plastic bag fee and teacher-housing legal work, and Commissioner Burns directed staff via Register of Deeds records to compile an inventory of unutilized school-board-owned real estate.

agenda_items.title: Closed Session (G.S. 143-318.11(a)(5)) and $100,000 Property Opening Bid Authorization
agenda_items.discussion_summary: With four commissioners present (Burns, Carter, Jacobs, Howerton; Allam not recorded on roll call), the Board voted 4-0 to enter closed session to instruct staff on property acquisition and employment contract negotiations under G.S. 143-318.11(a)(5). Returning to open session at 03:29:21, the Board voted 4-0 to authorize staff to submit an opening bid of $100,000 to acquire the discussed real property parcel and respond to upset bids as needed.

votes.item_title: Motion to Suspend the Rules for NCACC Voting Delegate Appointment During Work Session
votes.notes: Necessary to act on NCACC 115th Annual Conference voting delegate designations at a work session.
votes.discussion_detail: Ahead of the upcoming NCACC annual conference, the Board voted 5-0 by roll call to suspend its rules so it could formally designate its voting delegate and alternate during the August 1 work session.

votes.item_title: Appoint Wendy Jacobs as Voting Delegate and Nimasheena Burns as Alternate for NCACC 115th Annual Conference
votes.notes: Wendy Jacobs designated primary voting delegate; Nimasheena Burns designated alternate.
votes.discussion_detail: Following rules suspension, the Board unanimously voted 5-0 by roll call to name Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs as Durham County's primary voting delegate and Commissioner Nimasheena Burns as alternate for the NCACC 115th Annual Conference.

votes.item_title: Motion to Enter Closed Session Under G.S. 143-318.11(a)(5) (Real Property Acquisition / Employment Contract)
votes.notes: Nida Allam not recorded on closed-session roll call.
votes.discussion_detail: The Board voted 4-0 by roll call to enter closed session pursuant to G.S. 143-318.11(a)(5) to instruct staff regarding real property purchase terms and an employment contract.

votes.item_title: Authorize Staff to Enter $100,000 Opening Bid for Property Purchase and Respond to Upset Bids
votes.notes: Authorized County Manager to execute all transaction documents; ASR transcribed parcel reference as 'possible id 717'. Nida Allam absent from post-closed vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Upon reconvening in open session at 03:29:21, the Board moved, seconded, and voted 4-0 by roll call to authorize staff to submit an opening bid of $100,000 for the parcel discussed in closed session, respond appropriately to any upset bids, and empower the County Manager to execute closing documents.

meetings.title: BOCC Work Session August 1, 2022 Part 1
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over Part 1 of the August 1, 2022 BOCC Work Session with all five commissioners present. The Board heard citizen comments urging ARPA funding for permanent re-entry housing and protesting DSS Child Protective Services actions in the Wynn/Nguyen case, prompting Chair Howerton to remind the audience that commissioners cannot intervene in active legal proceedings. County Manager Kimberly Sowell then led a review of upcoming August consent agenda items—sparking extended commissioner questions on Adult Drug Treatment Court funding and Lincoln Community Health Center's $10 MAT co-pays (22-0432), Wellpath Detention Center medical staffing increases (22-0446), and Durham Pre-K's planned 86-student childcare center at 300/500 East Main Street (22-0450). Finally, Research Triangle Foundation leadership presented the annual Hub RTP and Boxyard update highlighting $4.7 billion in announced RTP private investment, 42.5% MWBE participation, and $15.3 million spent of Durham County's $20 million infrastructure commitment.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Public Charge, and Citizen Comments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton called the work session to order and read the public charge. Leticia Soria requested ARPA funds for permanent re-entry housing, while Operation Stop CPS advocates Amanda Wallace, Samantha Nguyen/Wynn, and Kiki Woods protested DSS child removals in the Wynn/Nguyen case; Chair Howerton clarified for the audience that elected commissioners cannot legally intervene in ongoing custody proceedings.

agenda_items.title: August Consent Agenda Review
agenda_items.discussion_summary: County Manager Kimberly Sowell reviewed 18 consent agenda items including Stanford L. Warren Library testing (22-0429, $74,947.40), enterprise IT renewals (22-0430, $456,465.90), Adult Drug Treatment Court ABC grant (22-0432, $42,500), Youth Home commissioning (22-0438, $74,443), Library Techmobile LSTA grant (22-0445, $79,750), Wellpath jail healthcare contract adjustment (22-0446, $292,806), HCCBG aging funding (22-0447), Durham Pre-K CCSA contract (22-0450), Grown in Durham (22-0452), ~2.4M in NC DHHS public health rollovers (22-0454-0456), and an RDU Airport FAA grant (22-0460). Commissioners questioned using opioid settlement funds to eliminate $10 MAT co-pays at Lincoln, Wellpath vacancy contingencies, and a planned 14,000-sq-ft / 86-child facility at 300/500 East Main Street.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0442: Annual Update on Hub RTP and Boxyard RTP
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Economic Development Manager Andy Miracle alongside Research Triangle Foundation leaders Scott Levitan, Linda Hall, and Sarah Chick reported $15.3 million spent of Durham County's $20 million Hub RTP infrastructure commitment (with the parking deck's $9.4M budget expected to yield savings), 42.5% MWBE participation across ~$105M in infrastructure, $4.7 billion in announced RTP private investment, and carbon-neutral-by-2050 targets alongside DEI and HBCU initiatives. meetings.title: BOCC Work Session August 1, 2022 Part 2
meetings.executive_summary: Note: Although archived under the date and title 'BOCC Work Session August 1, 2022 Part 2', the recording and transcript capture Durham County's April 4, 2022 Work Session presided over by Chair Brenda A. Howerton with all five commissioners present. After reading two emailed citizen comments on My Brother's Keeper Durham and Holton Career & Resource Center transit access and reviewing 13 consent items (22-0156 through 22-0209)—including Stanford L. Warren Library waterproofing (22-0189) and seven ambulances (22-0202)—the Board held extended work-session briefings on youth and community mental health (22-018), black maternal health disparities (22-0215), a revised $550.2M 2022 General Obligation Bond / FY22-31 CIP proposal lowering projected tax impact from 3.5 cents to 2.5 cents (22-0217), and Triangle J COG's Greater Triangle Commuter Rail Opportunity Analysis (22-0206). Commissioners pressed for actionable commitments for community doulas and teen-mom nonprofits, scrutinized DPS green-bond audits and surplus property reuse, and debated whether commuter rail justifies its regional cost before adjourning cleanly without taking substantive policy votes.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, MLK Remembrance, Public Charge, Citizen Comments, and Consent Agenda Review
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton opened with a moment of silence marking the 54th anniversary of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.'s assassination (April 4) and read emailed comments from Dwaren Langley on My Brother's Keeper Durham and Chris Tiffany on transit access to evening meetings. County Manager Kimberly Sowell then reviewed 13 consent items (22-0156 to 22-0209), including NCDHHS school health nursing funds ($262,706), Bioquell EMS ambulance sanitizers (22-0185), $1.58M Stanford L. Warren Library waterproofing and Muter Construction contract (22-0189, eight-to-ten-month timeline), utility contracts, seven ambulances without currently available anti-idling units (22-0202), Bull City Community Schools impact data (22-0204), Immigrant & Refugee Affairs ILA (22-0207), and a Library Foundation grant.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-018: Youth Trauma and Community Mental Health Crisis Briefing
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Dr. Ernestine Briggs-King (Duke / Center for Child & Family Health), Tara Bohley (UNC School of Social Work), and Ann Oshel (Alliance Health) presented data on pandemic trauma, youth suicide surges (citing a 57% jump from 2007-2018 and Black children under 13 dying by suicide at over twice the rate of white peers), insurance/navigation pathways, and Medicaid Transformation toward Tailored Plans and a statewide foster-care carve-out RFP. Commissioners demanded county-level service gap mapping, telehealth/broadband parity, County 911 behavioral health integration, and action to deploy a previously budgeted $1 million in uncommitted mental health funds.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0215: Black Maternal Health Update and Community Doula Partnership
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Health Director Rod Jenkins, Nursing Director Hattie Wood, Deputy Director Liz Stevens, Duke MFM specialist Dr. Maria Small, and community leaders Joy Lampkin Foster, Joy Spencer, Maya Jackson (MAAME Inc.), and Tamika Brown (HEARTS) detailed severe racial disparities—noting Black women face 3-4x higher pregnancy-related mortality, 48% higher preterm birth risk in NC, and worsening preterm trends locally—alongside requests for a full-time maternal nurse educator, County/Detention Center doula MOUs, home blood pressure cuffs, an on-site ultrasonographer, and direct equitable funding for Black-led CBOs. Tension emerged as Commissioner Nimasheena Burns and community presenters criticized a year of meetings without firm financial commitments, while Chair Howerton directed General Manager Joanne Pierce to schedule a focused follow-up ahead of budget adoption.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0217: FY22-31 Capital Improvement Program and Proposed November 2022 $550.2M GO Bond Referendum
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Director Keith Lane and General Manager Claudia Hager presented a revised 10-year CIP trimming projected FY24 property-tax impact from 3.5 cents to 2.5 cents ($88/year on a $350,000 home) by deferring DSS Main and select IS&T/renewable items while fully funding the $550.2M November 2022 GO Bond request: $423.5M for DPS, $112.7M for Durham Tech (life sciences, health sciences, and campus boundary land acquisition), and ~$14M for the Museum of Life and Science. Museum CEO Carrie Heinonen, Durham Tech President J.B. Buxton, and DPS Construction Director Frederick Davis II detailed project readiness, while commissioners probed Low-Income Homeowners Relief adjustments, Board of Elections space costs, $40M green-bond email advocacy versus completed energy audits, and surplus school parcel reuse.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0206: Greater Triangle Commuter Rail Opportunity Analysis (TJCOG) and Commissioner Directives/Comments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Triangle J COG Director John Hodges-Coppel and GoTriangle's Jay Heikes presented land-use, affordable-housing (2,700 legally restricted and NOAH corridor units; 15% with expiring covenants), and travel-market analyses showing 4% of four-county land holds 30% of primary jobs and 96,000 daily Wake-Durham inter-county commuters. Commissioner Burns questioned the commuter rail rationale for low-wage bus riders while Jacobs, Carter, and Howerton debated first-mile/last-mile links and South Florida rail lessons; afterward, Chief of Staff Drew Cummings reviewed directives and Burns criticized inaccurate public claims by a school board member regarding teacher pay and affordable-housing advocacy while requesting a farewell proclamation for retiring Duke basketball coach Mike Krzyzewski.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / No substantive votes (adjourned by roll call)

disagreements.issue: Urgency of Direct County Funding Commitments for Community-Based Black Maternal Health Organizations
disagreements.summary: After community-based doula and teen-parent organizations described nearly a year of meetings without firm county commitments while Black maternal and infant outcomes worsened, commissioners differed on how quickly and concretely to respond during the work session.
disagreements.side_a_position: Defer formal funding commitments until General Manager Joanne Pierce meets with staff and CBOs to prepare concrete budget proposals.
side_a_arguments: Work sessions are designed for listening and information gathering rather than making immediate budget appropriations on the dais.
Staff and CBOs should meet offline to distill clear, succinct dollar asks ahead of the upcoming budget cycle.
disagreements.side_b_position: The Board must act urgently now rather than continuing endless meetings after already leaving a $1M mental-health commitment and last year's Hear Her recommendations unimplemented.
side_b_arguments: Babies and mothers are still dying nearly a year after the June 3, 2021 presentation without dedicated action steps.
Silos between hospital systems, Public Health, and Black-led grassroots providers cannot persist without direct funding and written County commitments.
disagreements.resolution: Chair Howerton directed General Manager Joanne Pierce to convene the CBOs and return concrete funding proposals for the upcoming FY23 budget cycle.

disagreements.issue: Adding a $40 Million DPS Green Energy Bond Request Before Energy Audits Are Completed
disagreements.summary: Commissioner Wendy Jacobs pressed for clarity on whether DPS's $423.5M bond package adequately funded its renewable energy goals and green-bond line items, while Commissioner Nimasheena Burns and DPS Director Frederick Davis II cautioned against adding an unvetted $40M figure prior to energy audits.
disagreements.side_a_position: Wait for DPS's funded internal energy audits before adding another $40M onto taxpayers beyond the hard-won reduction to a 2.5-cent bond tax rate.
side_a_arguments: No board or school-board advocate could explain what the $40M green-bond email campaign specifically covered, and installing solar before upgrading windows and insulation is inefficient.
Staff worked hard to bring the CIP bond tax impact down from 3.5 cents to 2.5 cents for residents.
disagreements.side_b_position: Ensure DPS's modernization and energy-efficiency/generation commitments are explicitly tracked and adequately funded through clear CIP or audit-backed line items.
side_b_arguments: County staff created a transparent dedicated renewable-energy line item, and DPS should confirm its 2030/2050 carbon-reduction goals are similarly resourced.
Once DPS completes its energy audit, future two-year CIP updates can incorporate vetted renewable energy projects.
disagreements.resolution: Budget staff and DPS clarified that $3M in 2016 bonds was already allocated for Lyons Farm solar and a districtwide energy audit, leaving future green-energy allocations for the subsequent CIP update once the audit concludes.

disagreements.issue: Rationale and Equity of Commuter Rail Investments vs. Local Bus and Micro-Transit Priorities
disagreements.summary: Following Triangle J COG's Opportunity Analysis briefing, Commissioner Nimasheena Burns challenged the equity rationale for prioritizing expensive commuter rail over local bus service, while Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs and Chair Brenda A. Howerton emphasized regional job connectivity and public-private transit-oriented development.
disagreements.side_a_position: Pursue a regional multimodal rail spine paired with public-private TOD partnerships and dedicated first-mile/last-mile connectors so Durham residents can reach Triangle job centers.
side_a_arguments: Eight of the region's top ten job hubs, major universities, and 37% of Durham's legally restricted affordable housing lie within the corridor.
South Florida's Tri-Rail and Brightline demonstrate that electric shuttles, joint development value capture, and multi-county alignment can serve both riders and regional growth.
disagreements.side_b_position: Question whether commuter rail serves low-income bus riders earning under $40,000 or leaves behind local bus rapid transit and neighborhood bus connections.
side_b_arguments: Few of the 9,000 downtown apartments or corridor jobs serve very-low-income residents without guaranteed affordable fares and simultaneous BRT/feeder investments.
Commissioners remain skeptical that four separate governments will build feeder bus rapid transit in tandem with rail, risking low-income neighborhoods being left behind.
disagreements.resolution: Informational discussion ended without a vote; staff noted the Durham County Transit Plan update later in 2022 would weigh both bus and commuter rail allocations.

meetings.title: BOCC - July 11, 2022 - Regular Session
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over the July 11, 2022 Regular Session with all five commissioners present. The Board unanimously approved June 13 minutes (5-0), celebrated seven 2022 NACo Achievement Awards (22-0420), approved the consent agenda 5-0, and received a COVID-19 and monkeypox briefing (22-0405). In item 22-0421, following statutory public hearings, the Board adopted three General Obligation bond orders totaling $550,240,000—$423,505,000 for Durham Public Schools (5-0), $112,740,000 for Durham Technical Community College (5-0), and $13,995,000 for the Museum of Life and Science (4-0-1, Commissioner Nimasheena Burns recusing due to Museum board membership)—and called the November 8 special bond referendum. Following a sharply divided public hearing on Community Cats/TNVR (22-0394) pitting animal welfare groups against Audubon conservationists and Sheriff's Animal Services, Commissioners Carter, Burns, and Jacobs resolved a board disagreement by voting 5-0 to adopt the AWAC ordinance framework as a model while directing staff, the Sheriff's Office, APS, and nonprofits to return operational procedures within roughly six months rather than lifting trap permits immediately.

agenda_items.title: Announcements, Citizen Comments, and Approval of Minutes (June 13, 2022)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Commissioners announced the BULLS BioWork Academy, NACo committee participation, and August 15 ARPA grant deadlines. Citizen speakers included AWAC chair Jan Paul clarifying Community Cat/TNVR ordinance terms and Operation Stop CPS advocates Amanda Wallace and Samantha Nguyen regarding the Wynn children, after which the Board approved the June 13 work session and regular session minutes 5-0.

agenda_items.title: Ceremonial Recognition (22-0420: Seven 2022 NACo Achievement Awards) and Consent Agenda Approval
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton recognized Durham County departments for winning seven 2022 NACo Achievement Awards: Durham County Transit Plan, Tax Administration Chatbot, Board of Elections Ballot Tracking, DSS LIHR, DSS ERAP, Durham County Library Innovation League, and EMS Mobile Integrated Healthcare/Community Paramedicine. Commissioners thanked IS&T, DSS, Tax, Elections, Library, and EMS staff before voting 5-0 to approve Consent Agenda items 22-0321 through 22-0428.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0405: COVID-19 and Monkeypox Public Health Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Health Director Rod Jenkins reported 776 weekly COVID-19 cases (241.41 per 100,000), 343 cumulative deaths, 53.6% BA.5 variant dominance, newly started 0-5 pediatric vaccinations, and Durham's selection among North Carolina's first seven counties to receive monkeypox vaccine doses.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing 22-0421: 2022 General Obligation Bond Orders ($550,240,000 Total) and Referendum Resolutions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Deputy County Manager Claudia Hager presented the $550,240,000 General Obligation Bond package (projected 2.5-cent property tax impact; 2.3535% net debt ratio). After public hearings—where three residents supported and Ryan Calloway opposed the school bond over past accountability, while Duke Health, Novo Nordisk, Made in Durham, and Chamber leaders backed the Durham Tech bond—the Board adopted the $423,505,000 School Bond Order (5-0), the $112,740,000 Community College Bond Order (5-0), and the $13,995,000 Museum Bond Order (4-0-1, Nimasheena Burns abstaining), and passed corresponding November 8 special bond referendum resolutions.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed (Schools & DTCC 5-0; Museum 4-0-1 with Burns abstaining)

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing 22-0394: Proposed Animal Control Ordinance Amendment (Community Cats / TNVR)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Interim County Attorney Willie Darby presented the Animal Welfare Advisory Committee's draft ordinance removing legal barriers to Trap-Neuter-Vaccinate-Return (TNVR), reducing holding periods to 72 hours, and ending breed-only dangerous-dog designations, alongside 8 written comments (4 for, 4 against) and 123 petition cards in support. Animal welfare advocates (Best Friends, IAR, APS, HSUS) clashed with Sheriff's Animal Services Lt. Wendy Penner (citing staffing limits and 171 nuisance calls at one Treyburn address) and Audubon leaders Andrew Hudson and Barbara Driscoll (citing ~2B annual bird deaths and the Migratory Bird Treaty Act). Commissioners resolved an internal disagreement over immediate permit repeal versus operational planning by voting 5-0 to adopt the AWAC draft as a model while directing stakeholders to establish TNVR procedures within roughly six months.

agenda_items.title: Board and Commission Appointments and Closed Session
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Attorney Darby read ballot appointments for the ABC Board (2 seats including Daniel Edwards), Durham Convention Center Authority (Nicole Thompson), Women's Commission (2 seats), and JCPC (Alex Turtil Rosario). At 03:49:29, the Board voted 5-0 to enter closed session under G.S. 143-318.11(a)(5) and (a)(3) (regarding Magritte/McGruder v. Durham County Government, 20 CVS 330058), returning at 04:24:47 to give staff directions and adjourn.

votes.notes: Directs notice of special referendum and notification to the Durham County Board of Elections for the November 8, 2022 ballot.

votes.item_title: Adopt AWAC Animal Control Ordinance Draft as a Model and Direct Development of TNVR Implementation Regulations Within ~6 Months (Item 22-0394)
votes.notes: Compromise drafted during deliberation reconciling Carter's immediate-TNVR push with Burns' operational concerns and Jacobs' timeline accountability.
votes.discussion_detail: After an intense public hearing and 30-minute board deliberation over whether to immediately lift Sheriff trapping permit restrictions so volunteers could launch TNVR right away, Commissioner Carter modified her motion to adopt the AWAC draft ordinance as a model and direct County staff to convene the Sheriff's Office, AWAC, APS, and local nonprofits to finalize operational procedures and budget/facility plans within roughly six months, passing 5-0.

votes.notes: Upon returning to open session at 04:24:47, the Board noted it had given directions to staff before adjourning.
votes.discussion_detail: Following Boards and Commissions appointments, the Board voted 5-0 by roll call to enter closed session to instruct negotiators on real property/employment terms and consult legal counsel regarding litigation (20 CVS 330058).

disagreements.issue: Immediate Permit Repeal vs. Structured Six-Month Operational Rollout for Community Cat (TNVR) Ordinance Amendment (22-0394)
disagreements.summary: Following divided public testimony from animal welfare advocates (supporting immediate TNVR), Audubon conservationists (opposing feral colonies), and Sheriff's Animal Services (warning of staffing and nuisance constraints), Commissioners Heidi Carter, Nimasheena Burns, and Wendy Jacobs debated whether to lift trapping permit restrictions immediately or establish Sheriff-agency procedures first.
disagreements.side_a_position: Immediately adopt the AWAC ordinance language lifting Sheriff trapping permit restrictions so volunteer nonprofits can begin TNVR right away while final implementation rules are refined.
side_a_arguments: APS is at full capacity and still forced to euthanize healthy cats because existing ordinance rules restrict nonprofits from conducting TNVR.
Independent nonprofits and volunteer veterinarians are ready to begin trapping, spay/neutering, and vaccinating cats immediately at no immediate County cost.
disagreements.side_b_position: Do not immediately remove trapping permits or assign open-ended responsibilities before Sheriff's Office buy-in, funding, holding space, nuisance remedies, and a firm ~6-month timeline are established.
side_b_arguments: The Sheriff's Office has already stopped trapping due to overcrowding and lacks staff/equipment; shifting work immediately to outside groups without contracts, funding, or enforceable rules creates accountability and citizen-nuisance gaps.
Open-ended 'later date' ordinance language lacks urgency—staff must set a clear ~6-month deadline (targeting early 2023) with all stakeholders at the table.
disagreements.resolution: Commissioner Carter agreed to withdraw immediate implementation in favor of a compromise motion—adopted 5-0 at 03:44:52—adopting the AWAC ordinance draft as a model and directing staff to work with the Sheriff's Office, AWAC, APS, and nonprofits to finalize procedures within roughly six months.

meetings.title: BOCC Special Session - July 1, 2022
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton convened a brief July 1, 2022 special session with Commissioners Nida Allam, Nimasheena Burns, and Heidi Carter present (Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs received an excused absence by a 4-0 vote) to introduce the 2022 General Obligation Bond orders and set July 11 public hearings (Item 22-0414). Clerk Monica Wallace introduced bond orders for $423,505,000 in school bonds, $117,740,000 (initially stated) for Durham Technical Community College bonds, and $13,995,000 for Museum of Life and Science bonds, and the Board adopted resolutions setting public hearings (4-0 for schools and community college; 3-0 with Commissioner Burns abstaining for the museum). Before adjournment, County Manager Kimberly Sowell caught a $5 million typo in the agenda/resolution for Durham Tech, confirming the LGC application and total referendum figure of $550,240,000 reflected $112,740,000 for Durham Tech rather than $117,740,000. Commissioners promptly voted 4-0 to amend the prior motion so both the bond order introduction and public hearing resolution reflected the accurate $112,740,000 amount.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Public Charge, and Excused Absence for Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton called the special session to order with four commissioners on the line and read the public charge. Commissioner Heidi Carter moved and Commissioner Nimasheena Burns seconded granting an excused absence for Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs, which passed 4-0.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0414: Introduction of 2022 General Obligation Bond Orders and Resolutions Setting Public Hearings
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Clerk Monica Wallace formally introduced three General Obligation Bond orders: $423,505,000 for Durham Public Schools, $117,740,000 (as printed in the draft resolution) for Durham Technical Community College, and $13,995,000 for the Museum of Life and Science. The Board voted 4-0 to adopt the resolution calling public hearings for the School and Community College bond orders, and 3-0 (with Commissioner Nimasheena Burns abstaining due to her Museum board service) for the Museum bond order.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0414 (Amendment): Correction of Durham Technical Community College Bond Amount from $117,740,000 to $112,740,000
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Before adjournment, County Manager Kimberly Sowell asked staff to verify whether the Durham Tech bond order was $117,740,000 or $112,740,000, revealing that the agenda and draft resolution contained a typo whereas the application submitted to the Local Government Commission and the total referendum package of $550,240,000 used $112,740,000. On legal advice, the Board adopted an amendment clarifying that both the introduction of the Community College bond order and the public hearing resolution were for $112,740,000.
