meetings.title: BOCC - June 27, 2022 - Regular Session
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over the June 27, 2022 regular session with Commissioners Nida Allam, Nimasheena Burns, and Heidi Carter present (Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs had an excused absence). The Board recognized the Stormwater and Erosion Control Division's 2022 state large-program excellence award, highlighted an additional $1 million for Urban Ministries of Durham, and approved the 14-item consent agenda 4-0. Commissioners received a legal and timeline update on the $550.24 million 2022 General Obligation Bond referendum—emphasizing strict statutory prohibitions against elected officials and staff advocating for the bond—and approved 4-0 a multi-year ARPA grant ordinance (Item 22-0377) ahead of launching the County's 40-day nonprofit RFP window on July 5. Following a closed session, the Board voted 4-0 to approve a $2,000 housing allowance amendment to the County Manager's contract and to expand the County Attorney's contracting authority up to $75,000 for outside counsel representing individual-capacity claims against two County employees.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Announcements, and Recognition of Durham Tech Award
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton called the meeting to order, noted Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs' excused absence, and had Clerk Monica Wallace read community announcements including summer meals, Eno Fest, and Agricultural Economic Development grant workshops. Commissioner Burns also recognized Durham Tech for receiving El Centro Hispano's 2022 Community Award.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0282: Durham County Erosion Control Program State Award of Excellence
agenda_items.discussion_summary: NC Department of Environmental Quality program manager Julie Coco presented the 2022 Large Program Award of Excellence to Durham County's Stormwater and Erosion Control Division, praising its 3.5 FTEs overseeing nearly 250 projects across 2,600 acres and its transition to paperless Bluebeam reviews, online Paymentus fee collection, and GIS mobile inspections. Division Manager Ryan Eaves introduced staff and Commissioner Heidi Carter thanked the team for protecting Durham County's waterways.

agenda_items.title: Approval of Consent Agenda (Items 22-0346 through 22-0412)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: No consent items were pulled, though Commissioner Nimasheena Burns highlighted an item providing an additional $1 million to Urban Ministries to support unhoused and underserved residents. Later in the meeting at 01:40:39, County Manager Sowell confirmed that Item 22-0412 had been updated prior to the vote to extend Alliance Behavioral Health's deadline to return unspent funds from September 5 to September 15.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0402: 2022 General Obligation Bond Referendum Process Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: General Manager Claudia Hager reviewed the $550.24 million GO bond timeline—including the June 19 notice of intent, July 1 special meeting to introduce bond orders, July public hearing, LGC review, and November 8 election—noting an estimated 2.5-cent tax rate impact. Deputy County Manager/Communications Director Deborah Craig-Ray and County Attorney Willie Darby outlined the independent Blue Ribbon Committee's advocacy role and cautioned commissioners and staff (citing a recent Guilford County dispute) that they may share factual information but cannot use County funds or official capacities to advocate for or against the bond.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0377: ARPA Funding Update and Multi-Year Grant Ordinance Approval
agenda_items.discussion_summary: General Manager Claudia Hager presented an update on the County's $62 million American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) allocation, noting $2.2 million projected expenditure in the current year (prioritizing FEMA reimbursement where eligible), $6.8 million budgeted for school nurses, housing security, DA/public defender caseload relief, and Pre-K, and coordinated broadband RFP extensions ahead of July 2022 NC GREAT Grant awards. Hager announced the 40-day community nonprofit ARPA RFP would open July 5 through August 15 with virtual office hours, while commissioners stressed rural broadband survey outreach in Rougemont/Bahama and strict reporting accountability to avoid overlapping awards across City and County processes.

agenda_items.title: Boards and Commissions Appointments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff announced 19 appointments across 12 boards and commissions, including appointments to the Animal Welfare Advisory Committee, Bicycle and Pedestrian Advisory Commission, Citizen Advisory Committee, Criminal Justice Advisory Committee, Durham Hospital Corporation Board of Trustees, Women's Commission, Cultural Advisory Board, Planning Commission, Sports Commission, Environmental Affairs Board (correcting a ballot misprint that had listed the four appointees under Women's Commission), Historic Preservation Commission, and Juvenile Crime Prevention Council.

agenda_items.title: Closed Session and Post-Closed Session Actions (County Manager Contract & County Attorney Authority)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The Board entered closed session under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(4), (a)(6), and (a)(3) (including *Antonio Dar... v. Durham County EMS, Angela Garnish, Aubrey Reinhardt, Brandon Reinhardt et al.*). Upon reconvening at 02:37:59, commissioners approved two motions 4-0: amending the County Manager's contract to provide a $2,000 housing allowance in exchange for a multi-year service commitment, and amending the County Attorney's contracting authority up to $75,000 for legal representation of individual-capacity claims against two County employees.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 4-0 (Closed Session and both post-session motions)

votes.notes: Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs absent (excused).
votes.discussion_detail: Following an ARPA implementation, broadband RFP/GREAT Grant, and July 5–August 15 nonprofit RFP update, the Board adopted the multi-year grant budget ordinance appropriating the County's ARPA funds by a 4-0 vote.

votes.notes: Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs absent (excused).
votes.discussion_detail: The Board voted 4-0 to enter closed session to discuss economic development incentives, personnel qualifications/performance, and attorney-client privileged litigation matters.

votes.notes: Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs absent (excused). Transcript ASR rendered 'housing allowance' as 'housing alliance'.
votes.discussion_detail: Following closed session, the Board voted 4-0 to amend the County Manager's contract to provide a $2,000 housing allowance for the duration of her employment in exchange for a multi-year service commitment to Durham County Government.

votes.notes: Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs absent (excused). Transcript ASR rendered Allam as 'commissioner long'.
votes.discussion_detail: Commissioner Heidi Carter moved and Commissioner Nida Allam seconded amending the County Attorney's contracting authority to negotiate and execute a contract up to $75,000 for legal representation of individual-capacity claims against two County employees, passing 4-0.

meetings.title: BOCC - June 13, 2022 - Regular Session
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over the June 13, 2022 regular session with all five commissioners present. After an opening closed session, ceremonial proclamations for Resilient and Thriving Communities Week and June 2022 Pride Month, and consent agenda approval (excluding pulled Item 22-0296 and removing an emergency management ILA for City Community Safety), the Board adopted Unified Development Ordinance Omnibus Changes 17 (TC2100006) 5-0 after removing three small-lot provisions opposed by Preservation Durham. Commissioners then unanimously adopted (5-0) the historic >$750 million FY 2022–23 Annual Budget Ordinance (Item 22-0327) with no property tax increase, funding $11.8 million in County employee compensation increases, $177 million+ for Durham Public Schools (an ~$11 million increase), $12 million+ for Durham Tech, and $6.4 million for Durham Pre-K. The Board also approved 2022 GO bond pre-application resolutions ($550.24 million total across DPS, DTCC, and the Museum of Life and Science) and four nonprofit fund-balance appropriations (with required board-service abstentions) before unanimously passing the Triangle Bikeway resolution (Item 22-0296) despite sharp commissioner concerns over public engagement and transit equity.

agenda_items.title: Early Closed Session (Economic Development Incentives)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The Board convened early and voted 5-0 to enter closed session pursuant to NCGS 143-318.11(a)(4) to discuss the location or expansion of industries or businesses and tentative economic development incentives. Upon reconvening at 00:48:31, Chair Howerton reported that direction was given to staff, led opening remarks on Juneteenth, and led the Pledge of Allegiance.

agenda_items.title: Approval of May 23, 2022 Regular Session Minutes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Howerton called for edits to the May 23, 2022 regular session minutes. Hearing none, commissioners voted 5-0 to approve them.

agenda_items.title: Ceremonial Items: Thriving and Resilient Communities Week (22-0344) and June 2022 Pride Month (22-0345/22-035x)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Commissioner Heidi Carter read a proclamation designating Thriving and Resilient Communities Week, accepted by Public Health Director Rod Jenkins and Dr. Boone in recognition of trauma-informed ACEs work since 2018. Commissioners then presented a proclamation designating June 2022 as Pride Month in Durham County to LGBTQ Center of Durham representatives, noting the County's nondiscrimination ordinance taking effect in July.

agenda_items.title: Approval of Consent Agenda (Excluding Pulled Item 22-0296)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs asked about an interlocal agreement with Emergency Management supporting the City's Community Safety Department, and staff confirmed that item had been pulled from the agenda for a future date. Chair Howerton pulled Item 22-0296 (Triangle Bikeway resolution) to discussion, and the remaining consent items passed 5-0.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0342: Public Hearing and Adoption of UDO Text Amendment Omnibus Changes 17 (TC2100006)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staffer Michael Stock presented UDO Omnibus Changes 17 (recommended 11-2 by the Planning Commission), noting that three small-lot amendments were removed after Preservation Durham raised concerns over potential demolitions of older homes and that staff revised sight-distance triangle and accessory structure provisions per Planning Commissioner comments. Commissioners Carter, Jacobs, and Burns asked about affordable housing compliance reporting, Expanding Housing Choice metrics, plain-language graphics for residents, and legislative advocacy against preemptive state laws; with no public speakers signed up, the Board adopted the ordinance and consistency statement 5-0.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0327: Adoption of FY 2022–23 Annual Budget Ordinance
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The Board unanimously adopted (5-0) the FY 2022–23 Annual Budget Ordinance exceeding $750 million—the largest in County history—without raising the property tax rate. Following the vote, commissioners highlighted $11.8 million for County employee COLAs, merit pay, and public safety salary increases, over $177 million for Durham Public Schools (an ~$11 million increase including $1 million added by the Board beyond the manager's recommendation), over $12 million for Durham Tech, $6.4 million for Durham Pre-K, expanded low-income homeowner tax relief, and a commitment by Commissioners Carter, Allam, and Burns to advance toward a $25/hour living wage for County and DPS classified staff.

agenda_items.title: Items 22-0379, 22-0383, 22-0384, & 22-0385: Budget Ordinance Amendments for External Organizations (NCGS 14-234.3 Compliance)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: In separate special votes complying with Session Law 2021-191 / NCGS 14-234.3, the Board approved four unassigned general fund balance appropriations: $1,953,341 for the NC Museum of Life and Science (4-0, Burns abstaining), $160,000 for Downtown Durham Inc. (4-0, Howerton abstaining), $76,000 for the Museum of Durham History (4-0, Allam abstaining), and $562,070 for Project Access of Durham (4-0, Allam abstaining).

agenda_items.title: Items 22-0357 & 22-0381: 2022 General Obligation Bond Referendum Pre-Application Resolutions (DPS, DTCC, and Museum of Life and Science)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The Board approved the first-step pre-application resolutions for the $550,240,000 General Obligation Bond referendum, allocating $423,505,000 to Durham Public Schools and $112,740,000 to Durham Technical Community College (5-0), and $13,995,000 to the Museum of Life and Science (4-0, with Commissioner Burns abstaining). Commissioners recognized DTCC President J.B. Buxton in attendance and noted the historic size of the education bond package.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0296: Pulled Consent Item — Resolution Supporting Regional Implementation of the Triangle Bikeway
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Howerton pulled Item 22-0296 to question DCHC MPO coordinator Dale McKeel on missing responses from contacted community organizations and why ATV facilities for youth were not addressed. Commissioner Burns criticized the Board's pattern of pushing bike-lane plans forward without sufficient outreach to bus-dependent residents, while Vice Chair Jacobs emphasized that the resolution commits no County funding toward the ~$63 million Durham/Orange segments and simply initiates regional planning; the resolution passed 5-0.

votes.discussion_detail: The Board voted unanimously by roll call at the start of the session to enter closed session regarding economic development incentives.

votes.item_title: Approval of May 23, 2022 Regular Session Minutes
votes.discussion_detail: No edits were offered to the May 23, 2022 regular session minutes, and the motion passed unanimously by roll call.

votes.item_title: Adoption of UDO Text Amendment Omnibus Changes 17 (TC2100006 / Item 22-0342)
votes.discussion_detail: Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs moved and Commissioner Nimasheena Burns seconded adopting the ordinance amending UDO Articles 2–10, 12, and 15–17 (with three small-lot provisions previously pulled at Preservation Durham's request); passed 5-0.

votes.item_title: Adoption of Statement of Consistency for UDO Text Amendment TC2100006 (Item 22-0342)
votes.discussion_detail: The Board unanimously adopted the statement of consistency pursuant to NCGS 160D-605 for UDO Omnibus Changes 17.

votes.item_title: Adoption of FY 2022–23 Annual Budget Ordinance (Item 22-0327)

votes.item_title: Resolution Supporting Regional Implementation of the Triangle Bikeway (Item 22-0296)
votes.discussion_detail: Following questions from Chair Howerton and Commissioner Burns about community outreach, youth ATV needs, and bus-integration equity, Vice Chair Jacobs moved the resolution supporting the regional vision for the Triangle Bikeway (committing no County funds), which passed 5-0.

disagreements.issue: Triangle Bikeway Resolution: Community Engagement, Transit Equity, and Recreational Priorities (Item 22-0296)
disagreements.summary: Although the Board ultimately adopted the non-binding Triangle Bikeway resolution 5-0, Chair Howerton and Commissioner Burns challenged the sufficiency of community outreach and questioned prioritizing bike corridors over bus integration and youth ATV recreation, while Vice Chair Jacobs urged approval as a necessary first planning step.
disagreements.side_a_position: Questioned rushing forward with bike-lane resolutions without documented community-organization feedback, bus-system integration, or safe facilities for youth riding ATVs.
side_a_arguments: The packet lacked responses from most contacted community organizations aside from the Durham Committee on the Affairs of Black People (Howerton).
Bikeways do not address youth racing ATVs on highways who need safe recreational spaces (Howerton).

Roughly 80% of bus riders are not commuting 20–30 miles on dark bike trails; the Board 'rams things through' on bike lanes and must ensure intentional outreach and bus integration going forward (Burns).
disagreements.side_b_position: Approve the resolution as an essential initial regional planning step that commits zero County funding.
side_b_arguments: The resolution only endorses the regional vision so partners like Wake County, RTP Foundation, and NCDOT can explore future phased funding for the ~$63 million Durham/Orange segments.
Approving the plan is procedurally required before any future implementation or grant applications can occur.
disagreements.resolution: Staff confirmed the resolution committed no County funding and pledged to send additional outreach responses and explore ATV recreation separately; the Board approved the resolution 5-0.

meetings.title: BOCC Budget Work Session #4 - Monday, June 6, 2022
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over the FY 2022–23 budget work session (titled on YouTube as June 6, 2022 Budget Work Session #4, though speakers referenced May 17, 2022 primary election day during the broadcast), with all five commissioners present. Budget Director Keith Lane reviewed the manager's recommended budget featuring extraordinary revenue growth, a flat property tax rate, $6.4–$6.5 million in general fund ARPA support, 2.5%/3.5% employee COLAs, 3%–4% merit pay, and 36.7 new general fund FTEs, while cautioning that FY23 revenue spikes may not recur in FY24. CFO Susan Tezai presented fund-balance projections (39.08% total and 19.48% unassigned for FY22, maintaining the County's AAA management credit rating and 69.55 days of cash liquidity amid $8 million in pending FEMA reimbursements and $1.6 million in cyberattack recovery costs). Tax Administrator Dwane Brinson briefed the Board on the 2025 reappraisal kickoff, 1.25% holdbacks, and $719 million in partial exemptions, while HR Director Kathy Everett-Perry detailed rising turnover above 18% and proposed pay/benefit enhancements including paid family leave. Commissioners concluded by discussing the upcoming add/delete list, school funding flexibility, and Chair Howerton's request to see what cuts would be needed to add $2 million without raising taxes.

agenda_items.title: FY 2022–23 Recommended Budget Major Revenue and Expenditure Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Director Keith Lane presented the FY 2022–23 manager's recommended budget, highlighting extraordinary revenue growth driven by FY21–22 collections while maintaining a flat property tax rate. Key priorities included $6.4–$6.5 million of ARPA funding in the general fund, 2.5% COLAs for employees above $75,000 and 3.5% below $75,000, 3%–4% merit pay, focused EMS/public safety compensation adjustments, and 36.7 new general fund FTEs.

agenda_items.title: Fund Balance, Cash Liquidity, and Reserve Policy Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: CFO Susan Tezai reported that Durham County's 35% total / 16% unassigned fund-balance policy remains critical to maintaining its AAA rating, projecting FY22 fund balance at $269.6 million (39.08% total, 19.48% unassigned) and 69.55 days of operating cash on hand. She noted the County had filed nearly $8 million in FEMA COVID-19 claims with no reimbursement received yet and incurred ~$1.6 million in cyberattack recovery costs, and previewed future policy updates focusing on unassigned reserves and liquidity.

agenda_items.title: Tax Valuation, Holdbacks, Exemptions, and 2025 Reappraisal Preview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Tax Administrator Dwane Brinson reviewed property tax projections—including >3% real property growth, 8% personal property, and >15% motor vehicle growth—and explained the County's 1.25% holdback and $719 million in statutory partial exemptions (~$5.2 million in foregone revenue). Because current bills still rely on January 1, 2019 values ahead of the January 1, 2025 reappraisal, Commissioner Burns warned of severe sticker shock and displacement pressure on Black and lower-income homeowners, urging expansion of the Low-Income Homeowner Relief program.

agenda_items.title: Employee Compensation, Turnover, and New Benefits Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: HR Director Kathy Everett-Perry reported that County turnover climbed 3.9% above the 18% governmental benchmark with 302 employees eligible to retire in FY23, and noted that 83% of employees (earning ≤$75,000) would be eligible for up to 7.5% combined COLA/merit increases while 17% above $75,000 could receive up to 6.5%. She also detailed the County's $15/hour living wage floor (with the lowest actual employee at ~$16.78/hour) and proposed FY23 benefits including four weeks of paid family leave, five days of funeral leave, wellness clinic family access, and pet insurance, laying groundwork for a formal compensation philosophy.

agenda_items.title: Board Budget Q&A, Add/Delete Process, and DPS Funding Discussion
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff outlined the upcoming email Q&A and add/delete list workflow, explaining how Durham Public Schools receives current-expense allocations rather than PRC-earmarked funds. Commissioners discussed comparing per-pupil funding across counties (noting Wake County mixes debt service into reported totals), Vice Chair Jacobs praised a new $500,000 Public Art Fund allocation, and Chair Howerton asked staff to identify what cuts would be needed to free up $2 million for community priorities without raising taxes.

meetings.title: BOCC - Work Session - Monday, June 6, 2022 (Part 1)
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over Part 1 of the June 6, 2022 BOCC work session with all five commissioners present (no formal votes were taken). The Board heard citizen comments from Bike Durham urging faster capital transit delivery, reviewed consent agenda items for the upcoming regular session, and vetted Item 22-0323 to establish a two-phase independent, confidential County Ombuds Office with consultants from the Town of Chapel Hill. Commissioners also received an informational briefing on the Triangle Bikeway study ahead of the June 13 vote and engaged in an extended policy debate with City Transportation Director Sean Egan over the FY23 Transit Work Program, $10.8 million FTA-funded Durham Station upgrades ($2.7 million local match), City staffing requests, sidewalk cost-sharing, and how to deploy the ~$87–$100 million half-cent sales tax fund balance held for major regional transit projects.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order and Citizen Comments (Bike Durham on FY23 Transit Work Program)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton called the work session to order and read the public charge. Bike Durham board member Eric Landfried urged commissioners to work collaboratively with the City Council to fund additional transit project-delivery positions—noting projects like the Village Transit Center had been delayed since 2013—oppose project-by-project sidewalk cost-sharing, and require clear project charters.

agenda_items.title: Review of Consent Agenda Items for Upcoming Regular Session
agenda_items.discussion_summary: County Manager Kimberly Sowell walked through draft consent items including Justice Center courtroom AV upgrades ($136,073.96, Item 22-0272), $364,074 in NC DHHS funding for public health communicable disease nurses (Item 22-0278), Hoopla digital library services ($200k range, Item 22-0307), $40,000 for IS&T (Item 22-0319), a new County Attorney FTE (Item 22-0325), and MWBE/HUB certification efforts (Item 22-0345). Commissioners asked clarifying questions on public health hiring, library reporting, and MWBE certification.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0323: Discussion of Establishing a Durham County Ombuds Office
agenda_items.discussion_summary: General Manager Claudia Hager and Chapel Hill mediator-consultants Tiffany Sneed and Matthew Sullivan presented a proposal to create an independent, impartial, confidential Ombuds Office—starting with County employees in Phase 1 before expanding to residents in Phase 2. Commissioners Carter, Allam, Howerton, and Burns questioned whether reporting lines to the County Manager could compromise perceived independence, how the non-investigative role interacts with HR grievance policies, and whether a single FTE could handle countywide employee and public caseloads.

agenda_items.title: Triangle Bikeway Study Informational Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Transportation Manager Ellen Beckman and DCHC MPO coordinator Dale McKeel presented findings from the two-year Triangle Bikeway study ahead of the June 13 action item to endorse the regional plan. Commissioners Allam and Carter asked about trail amenities, while Chair Howerton and Commissioner Burns requested the full study report and raised questions about stakeholder participation.

agenda_items.title: City of Durham Transit Projects, Durham Station, and FY23 Transit Work Program Discussion
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Transportation Director Sean Egan presented schematic designs for Durham Station (15,000 daily riders; awarded $10.8 million federal FTA grant requiring a $2.7 million local match), the Better Bus Project covering 12 miles of sidewalk gaps and Fayetteville/Holloway corridor upgrades, Treyburn vanpools, and GoDurham Connect in East Durham. Commissioners engaged in an extensive debate with Egan and County Transportation Manager Ellen Beckman over whether half-cent transit sales tax revenues (~$30–$32 million/year with ~$87–$100 million accumulated fund balance) should cover City staffing and sidewalk work or require City cost-sharing to preserve funds for regional rail/BRT.

disagreements.issue: Durham County Transit Plan: City Staffing/Sidewalk Cost-Sharing vs. Utilizing $100M Transit Fund Balance
disagreements.summary: Commissioners and City/County transportation leaders disagreed over whether to require City of Durham cost-sharing for additional transit project-delivery staff and sidewalk improvements, and whether the accumulated ~$87–$100 million half-cent transit sales tax fund balance should be tapped to accelerate local bus/access projects or preserved for major regional transit investments.
disagreements.side_a_position: Require City cost-sharing for City transit staff and sidewalk improvements, establish clear tri-board financial/governance policies with GoTriangle, and preserve the transit sales tax fund balance for regional commuter rail or Bus Rapid Transit (BRT).
side_a_arguments: Durham County generates only ~$30–$32 million/year in transit revenues (potentially losing ~$25 million over 20 years from rental-car tax changes), so sidewalk repairs and amenities—basic city functions—should not crowd out core transit service and regional BRT/rail (Jacobs, Carter).
The ~$87–$100 million fund balance exists specifically because voters approved the sales tax for major regional projects like commuter rail (Jacobs).
Cost-sharing ensures 'skin in the game' and clear governance policies among the County, City, and GoTriangle (Howerton, Jacobs, County Manager staff Ellen Beckman).
disagreements.side_b_position: Support funding requested City transit staff positions without punitive cost-share delays and leverage the ~$100 million transit fund balance to deliver overdue bus stop, sidewalk, and corridor improvements immediately.
side_b_arguments: Without additional staffing capacity, $25–$35 million in transit corridor projects face 8%–10% annual construction cost escalation (~$1 million/year lost per year of delay) while transit-dependent riders (80% people of color, two-thirds zero-car households) wait for basic shelters and sidewalks (City Director Sean Egan, Bike Durham).
Approving requested staffing positions is critical so historically excluded neighborhoods do not remain left behind on overdue transit and shelter repairs (Allam).
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote was taken at the work session; Chair Howerton requested GoTriangle fund-balance documentation and staff continued developing formal cost-sharing and governance policies through the tri-board governance study.

meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over Part 1 of Budget Work Session #3 on June 3, 2022, with all five commissioners present for departmental FY 2022–23 budget reviews (no formal votes taken). Information Services & Technology (IS&T) reviewed four newly recommended FTEs and CIP technology replacements, while new ABC Board GM L. Sordell projected $61.43 million in revenue and a $2.5 million County distribution (with commissioners requesting an additional $100,000). Sheriff Clarence Birkhead outlined requests for an external Detention Center maintenance contract, a $735,000 (5%) pay adjustment to combat academy and officer attrition, and a 3% detention night-shift differential. Office of Emergency Services Director Jim Groves detailed ambulance fleet replacements, a proactive Fire Marshal commercial fee schedule (+$36,000 estimated revenue), increasing EMS billing from 157% to 200% of Medicare rates ($2.7–$3.8 million projected revenue), and detailing two County EMTs to the City's Community Safety crisis teams; General Manager Joanne Pierce also reviewed the newly created Community Intervention & Support Services (CISS) department and Soil & Water presented its Agricultural Economic Development Grant program.

agenda_items.title: Information Services & Technology (IS&T) Budget and CIP Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: CIO Greg Marrow presented IS&T's 'Run, Grow, Transform' FY23 budget, highlighting four newly awarded positions (two business analysts, one project manager, and one service desk technician) and upcoming CIP technology replacement needs. He noted IS&T remained below local government benchmarks at 3.0% of the County budget and 2.5% of total staffing compared to 4.7% and 4.8% industry averages.

agenda_items.title: Durham County ABC Board Budget Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: New ABC Board General Manager L. Sordell projected $61.43 million in gross revenue for FY23, reviewed store remodels, the new Highway 55 store and >$1.5 million upset bid on the old property, a Page Road/TW Alexander build, July 1 mixed-beverage delivery launch, and a 6% across-the-board staff raise. The ABC Board budgeted $2.5 million in County distributions (out of $3.78 million total local/law enforcement/rehab distributions), and commissioners discussed asking for an additional $100,000 distribution and potential County partnership on the vacated Fayetteville Street property.

agenda_items.title: Durham County Sheriff's Office Budget Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Sheriff Clarence Birkhead and command staff presented Priority #1—contracting with a third-party vendor to handle 24/7 Detention Center maintenance (HVAC, locks, elevators, plumbing) given General Services staffing shortages—and thanked the County Manager for recommending Priority #2 ($735,000 for a 5% law enforcement and detention pay adjustment) and Priority #3 (3% night-shift differential). Finance/HR staff showed that ongoing separations left the agency at a net 19-to-24-officer deficit even after graduating a 20-officer academy, while commissioners asked about SROs, mental health/opioid burdens in the jail, and state-mandated inmate housing.

agenda_items.title: Office of Emergency Services (EMS & Fire Marshal) Budget and Fee Schedule Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: OES Director Jim Groves and Fire Marshal Jason Shepherd presented ambulance fleet replacement plans (adding Stealth Power anti-idling and box remounting saving ~$100,000/year), a restructured proactive commercial Fire Marshal inspection fee schedule (~$36,000 net revenue increase), and a proposal to raise EMS billing rates from 157% to 200% of the Medicare fee schedule (projected to generate $2.7–$3.8 million to offset general fund costs and pay raises). Groves also outlined Mobile Integrated Healthcare expansion and OES's commitment to detail two rotating County EMTs to the City's Community Safety crisis teams.

agenda_items.title: Community Intervention & Support Services (CISS) Department Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: General Manager Joanne Pierce reviewed the newly formed CISS department uniting Bull City United (expanding from 17 to 25 staff across four additional census tracts via City ILA, with final six hires starting June 21), My Brother's Keeper, and Project BUILD gang prevention/intervention, requesting administrative support positions. Commissioners discussed developing community-based alternatives to youth detention and Chair Howerton urged clearer public communication so residents understand Bull City United's violence-mediation role.

agenda_items.title: Soil and Water Conservation District Agricultural Economic Development Grant Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Soil and Water staff and committee chair David Harris reviewed the Agricultural Economic Development Grant program ($75,000 budgeted in FY22 vs. consistently higher demand capped at $5,000 per farm/nonprofit and $1,000 per school). Commissioners Burns and Carter expressed support for increasing total grant funding, raising per-project caps, and considering non-food horticultural or organic soil incentives, while Vice Chair Jacobs questioned declining federal/state cost-share funding indicators on budget book page 110.

meetings.title: BOCC Budget Work Session #3 Part 2
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over Part 2 of Budget Work Session #3 on June 3, 2022 (with Commissioner Nimasheena Burns departing at 00:29:27; no formal votes taken). Soil and Water Conservation District staff presented the BETC/CCAP student green-infrastructure training program—highlighting a 20% environmental literacy gain across two participating schools—and requested a $68,919 Outreach Coordinator FTE alongside a community coalition ask of $200,000 to expand to four schools. Budget Director Keith Lane then walked commissioners through the FY 2022–23 Add/Delete list, detailing administrative grant adjustments, ~$800,000–$900,000 in general fund items potentially shifted to ARPA, and proposed additions including +$1 million for Durham Public Schools, +$146,000 for Bull City Community Schools, $50,000 for TJCOG Solarize, $50,000 for MWBE support, $125,000 for the Ombuds FTE, two $140,000 attorney positions, and $69,000 for Soil & Water, leaving a net ~$300,000–$400,000 balance covered by general fund balance with no tax rate increase. Commissioners differed briefly over hiring a full-time transportation attorney versus using outside legal consultants and deferred that personnel discussion to closed session.

agenda_items.title: Soil and Water BETC/CCAP Program Presentation and Outreach Coordinator Request
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Soil and Water staff detailed the four-week summer BETC/CCAP program, where certified high school teachers and students design and install state-spec rain gardens (~$45,000 per school/year), achieving a 20% increase in environmental literacy and workforce pathways. Staff requested a $68,919 Outreach Coordinator FTE, while Commissioner Heidi Carter referenced a coalition request from Matt Kopac and nine environmental groups for $200,000 (expanding from two to four schools and adding $80,000 to CCAP); Commissioner Allam requested greater language-equity outreach to public housing families and Vice Chair Jacobs praised workforce outcomes and flood-mitigation targeting in Braggtown.

agenda_items.title: FY 2022–23 Budget Add/Delete List Review
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Director Keith Lane presented the FY23 Add/Delete spreadsheet, noting net-zero administrative adjustments (+$450,000 maternal health grant, +$65,000 city-funded immigrant/refugee position, -$31,000 Pre-K adjustment, -$150,000 duplicate early childhood line) and removing a $625,000 Sheriff/Youth Home increase that County Manager Sowell clarified was a misunderstanding. Proposed additions included +$1 million for DPS (with DPS expected to tap its fund balance for the remainder of its $1.9 million request), +$146,000 for Bull City Community Schools, +$71,000 for Pre-K wraparound care, $50,000 for TJCOG Solarize, $50,000 for MWBE support, $125,000 for an Ombuds FTE, $140,000 for a general attorney, $140,000 for a transportation attorney, and $69,000 for Soil & Water, offset by shifting ~$800k–$900k to ARPA and potentially +$100,000 from the ABC Board—requiring ~$300,000–$400,000 from general fund balance while keeping the tax rate flat.

agenda_items.title: Discussion of Transportation Legal Counsel (In-House FTE vs. Consultants) and DPS Fund Balance
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs questioned adding a dedicated $140,000 transportation attorney FTE, suggesting the County could instead hire consultants or recruit transportation expertise into the already-proposed attorney slot to control recurring staff costs. Chair Brenda A. Howerton countered that ongoing GoTriangle disputes require dedicated in-house transportation counsel because the County lacks internal expertise, and the Board agreed to hold that staffing conversation for closed session after confirming DPS's willingness to use fund balance toward its remaining $0.9 million request.

disagreements.issue: In-House Transportation Attorney FTE vs. Outside Legal Consultants
disagreements.summary: Commissioners differed during the Add/Delete list review on whether to fund a dedicated $140,000 in-house transportation attorney FTE or rely on outside consultants / an existing proposed attorney position.
disagreements.side_a_position: Prefer using outside consultants or recruiting transportation expertise within the already-planned new attorney position to minimize ongoing FTE costs.
side_a_arguments: Adding another permanent FTE increases recurring County personnel costs when specialized transportation advice might be procured more cost-effectively via consultants or combined into the general attorney hire.
disagreements.side_b_position: Hire a dedicated in-house transportation attorney FTE to advise the County on GoTriangle and complex transit matters.
side_b_arguments: Ongoing GoTriangle issues are creating problems because Durham County government currently has no internal legal counsel with transportation expertise to advise the Board (Howerton).
General Manager Claudia Hager noted that hiring part-time or contractual legal talent at that level can be difficult compared to a full-time role that could later be re-evaluated through attrition.
disagreements.resolution: No decision was made during the open work session; Chair Howerton and Vice Chair Jacobs agreed to defer the personnel discussion to closed session ahead of the June 6 work session and June 13 budget vote.

meetings.title: Board of County Commissioners on 2022-06-02 9:00 AM - Budget Work Session - Day 3
meetings.executive_summary: At the June 2, 2022 Budget Work Session (Day 3) presided over by Chair Brenda A. Howerton, the Durham Board of County Commissioners held informational budget briefings with county departments and took no formal votes, with no split or contested votes occurring. After the County Manager previewed an agenda covering IS&T, the ABC Board ($2.5 million projected revenue), the Sheriff, EMS and Fire Marshal fee changes, the CISS program, Soil and Water, and an initial Add/Delete list, IS&T leadership reviewed four newly funded positions, upcoming ERP replacement planning for the 20-year-old SAP system, broadband expansion RFPs, and cybersecurity threats. Following a truncated middle portion of the transcript, staff briefed the Board on the joint City-County Community Intervention and Support Services (CISS) department—requesting roughly $337,000 in operational funding and vehicles to support an expansion from 7 to 25 positions under the City-County Interlocal Agreement, prompting commissioner questions about proportional City cost-sharing and community-based alternatives to youth detention. The captured session concluded with Soil and Water Conservation updates on over-subscribed Agricultural Economic Development Grants ($75,000 allocated against higher capped $5,000 requests), fluctuating state and federal cost-share funding, and the BETC/CCAP youth green-infrastructure training program.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order and Budget Work Session Agenda Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton called the Day 3 Budget Work Session to order, and commissioners briefly noted Pride Month ahead of a planned June 13 resolution. The County Manager outlined the day's schedule—including IS&T, ABC Board ($2.5 million budgeted county distribution), Sheriff, EMS and Fire Marshal fee changes, CISS, Soil and Water, and the first Add/Delete list covering items such as potential extra DPS funding and the Solarize program—while commissioners thanked budget staff for answering pre-meeting questions.

agenda_items.title: Information Services & Technology (IS&T) Budget, ERP, Broadband, and Cybersecurity
agenda_items.discussion_summary: IS&T staff presented their FY 2023 budget under the 'run, grow, and transform' framework, highlighting four newly awarded positions (two business analysts, one project manager, and one service desk technician) while noting IS&T remains below peer local-government averages in budget (3% vs. 4.7%) and staffing (2.5% vs. 4.8%). Presenters flagged upcoming fall capital lifecycle replacement needs, a business requirements analysis to replace the 20-year-old SAP enterprise resource planning (ERP) system, a broadband expansion RFP closing that month alongside ISP state GREAT grant applications, and heightened cybersecurity risks.

agenda_items.title: Community Intervention and Support Services (CISS) Operations and City-County ILA
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following a truncated middle segment of the transcript, staff discussed operational priorities for the joint City-County community safety/intervention department (CISS), including embedding equity, partnering with community-rooted organizations, launching a public-facing website with quarterly reports and incident maps, and reposting a key leadership role. Staff explained a ~$337,000 funding request and vehicle needs because the City-County Interlocal Agreement covered only straight salaries when expanding the team from seven to 25 staff across four census tracts without laptops, phones, training, or materials; commissioners asked about proportional City operational contributions and raised public-hearing calls for county-controlled, community-based youth services to phase out youth detention.

agenda_items.title: Soil and Water Conservation: Agricultural Grants, Cost-Share Trends, and BETC/CCAP
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Soil and Water staff reviewed the Agricultural Economic Development Grant program—noting allocations rose from $25,000 in 2018 to $75,000 the prior year while capped $5,000 applications from farmers and nonprofits continued to exceed funding—prompting a commissioner request for updated demand numbers ahead of upcoming budget decisions. Commissioners also questioned declining federal and state natural-resource funding indicators in the budget book (down from nearly $2 million in FY19), raised 'Save our Soil' advocates' proposal for soil-organic-content incentives, and heard an update on the BETC/CCAP program providing paid student work experience and green-infrastructure training.

meetings.title: BOCC - May 23, 2022 - Regular Session
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over the May 23, 2022 regular session with all five commissioners present, opening with a moment of silence for victims of the Buffalo, New York shooting and a Memorial Day proclamation. The Board approved the consent agenda 5-0 (including a separate 5-0 approval of pulled items for a grant-funded mobile public health medical unit and a 10% construction materials testing contingency) and voted 5-0 to approve Zoning Map Change Z2100013 (Parmer Sector 3 on So-Hi Drive, rezoning ~4.3 acres from Rural Residential to Science Research Park). Commissioners held the public hearing on the FY 2022–23 County Manager's Recommended Budget (Item 22-0308)—extending speaker time from one to two minutes by a 5-0 vote—hearing pleas for Sheriff's Office/detention pay raises, living wages, and renewable energy investments. Following presentations on COVID-19 (CDC Yellow level) and Family Connects Durham, and heated public testimony on Item 22-0291 (Community Cat TNVR Animal Control Ordinance), the Board voted 5-0 to advance the TNVR draft ordinance to a public hearing (subsequently amended post-closed session to July 11, 2022).

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Moment of Silence, Announcements, and Approval of Minutes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton called the meeting to order, read the public charge, asked Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs to lead the Pledge of Allegiance, and held a moment of silence for the victims of the Buffalo, New York shooting. Clerk Monica Wallace read community announcements, commissioners discussed pandemic business recovery grants ($21M Durham / $200M state) and rural broadband needs, and the Board approved prior May minutes 5-0.

agenda_items.title: Ceremonial Items: Memorial Day 2022 Proclamation and DSS Eligibility Workers Month Resolution
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Howerton read a Memorial Day 2022 proclamation honoring fallen military service members, accepted by Veteran Services representatives. Before the consent agenda, Vice Chair Jacobs also shared a DSS Board resolution proclaiming May 2022 as Eligibility Workers Month in recognition of income maintenance staff.

agenda_items.title: Approval of Consent Agenda (Including Pulled Items 22-0292 and 22-0286)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Commissioners pulled Item 22-0292 (grant-funded mobile public health medical unit) and Item 22-0286 (10% contingency for independent construction materials testing) for brief public explanations by Health Director Rod Jenkins and staff, and approved the remaining consent items 5-0. Immediately following the staff explanations, the Board voted 5-0 to approve Items 22-0292 and 22-0286.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing and Adoption of Zoning Map Change Z2100013 (Parmer Sector 3, 2102 & 2152 So-Hi Drive)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staffer Michael Stock and applicant attorney Worth Mills (Longleaf Law Partners) presented a general-use rezoning of ~4.3 acres from Rural Residential (RR) to Science Research Park (SRP) to resolve a 1989 split-zoning irregularity across the 51-acre parcel inside Research Triangle Park (recommended 10-0 by the Planning Commission). Commissioner Carter sought commitments on future So-Hi Drive bike facilities and stream/floodplain/tree protection during future site plan review, and the Board adopted the zoning ordinance and NCGS 160D-605 consistency statement 5-0.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0308: Public Hearing on FY 2022–23 County Manager's Recommended Budget
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The Board opened the public hearing on the FY 2022–23 recommended budget and voted 5-0 (on a motion by Commissioner Allam seconded by Commissioner Burns) to extend individual speaker time from one minute to two minutes. Speakers included detention and Sheriff's Office personnel (such as Annetta Page) urging competitive pay raises to address staffing crises, as well as advocates calling for renewable energy investments aligned with the County's 2018 clean energy resolution.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 5-0 (speaker time extension); Public hearing informational

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0303: Public Health COVID-19 Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Health Director Rod Jenkins reported 1,083 current cases, a seven-day moving average of 154 (down 9.53% from the prior week), 15.5% PCR positivity, and Durham County's move into the CDC 'Yellow' community level along with the broader Triangle. He answered commissioner questions on wastewater surveillance, five-day isolation guidance, pediatric vaccines (ages 5–11), and Paxlovid antiviral access.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0290: Update on Family Connects Durham
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Center for Child and Family Health leaders Robert Murphy and Dr. Karen Appleyard Harmony, nurse Karen Halpin, and parent Vanessa Diaz presented outcomes for Family Connects Durham, which has served over 20,000 Durham families since 2008 (1,366 visits and 1,600 referrals in 2021 with an 86% one-month connection rate and >$3 in emergency medical savings per $1 spent). Staff noted pandemic adaptations to telehealth and efforts to hire a new Spanish-speaking nurse to restore Hispanic participation rates.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0291: Proposed Amendment to Animal Control Ordinance (Community Cat TNVR Program)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: County Attorney Willie Darby presented the draft Animal Control Ordinance amendment developed with AWAC and Best Friends Animal Society to enable a future TNVR program while deferring operational implementation until costs and staffing are resolved. Although not a formal public hearing, citizens and officials spoke on both sides: Sheriff's Animal Services Sgt. Wendy Penner (citing 2,368 trap requests since 2012 and severe nuisance complaints) and Capt. Mark Manning (warning of 20% higher call volume and >$535k–$700k+ in staffing/spay-neuter costs), wildlife rehabilitators, and Sharon Cadell urged caution or opposition, while APS Director Shafonda Allen urged ending trap-and-euthanize practices. The Board voted 5-0 to accept the draft subject to edits and schedule a public hearing, and amended the motion after closed session to set the public hearing for July 11, 2022.

agenda_items.title: Boards and Commissions Appointments, Closed Session, and Excused Absence
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Attorney Darby announced appointments to the Bicycle and Pedestrian Advisory Commission (Monica Green), Women's Commission (Roberta Price), Durham Hospital Corporation Board of Trustees (Constanza Gomez-Jones, Hector Hidalgo, and Paul Moussa), and Racial Equity Commission (Jada Richardson). The Board voted 5-0 to enter closed session under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(5), reconvened with directions to staff, amended the TNVR public hearing date to July 11, 2022 (5-0), and approved an excused absence for Commissioner Heidi Carter on June 27, 2022 (5-0).
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 5-0 (Closed Session, TNVR date amendment, Excused Absence)

votes.discussion_detail: No edits were requested to the May 2 work session and May regular session minutes, and the motion passed unanimously by roll call.

votes.item_title: Approval of Pulled Consent Agenda Items 22-0292 (Mobile Medical Unit) and 22-0286 (10% Construction Materials Testing Contingency)
votes.discussion_detail: After staff explained that Item 22-0286 covers standard independent building-code materials testing and Health Director Rod Jenkins explained that Item 22-0292 is a grant-funded mobile clinic for outreach and immunizations, the Board approved both items 5-0.

votes.item_title: Adoption of Zoning Map Change Z2100013 Ordinance (Parmer Sector 3, 2102 & 2152 So-Hi Drive)
votes.discussion_detail: Following the public hearing on rezoning ~4.3 acres from Rural Residential (RR) to Science Research Park (SRP) to match the remainder of the 51-acre RTP parcel, Commissioner Carter adjusted her motion (after staff noted the ordinance must precede the consistency statement) to adopt the zoning map change, passing 5-0.

votes.item_title: Adoption of Statement of Consistency for Zoning Map Change Z2100013 (NCGS 160D-605)
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately after adopting the Z2100013 rezoning ordinance, the Board voted 5-0 by roll call to adopt the NCGS 160D-605 statement of consistency with the comprehensive plan.

votes.item_title: Procedural Motion to Extend Budget Public Hearing Speaker Time to Two Minutes (Item 22-0308)
votes.notes: Transcript ASR rendered Nida Allam as 'commissioner law' / 'commissioner alone'.
votes.discussion_detail: After Chair Howerton proposed limiting speakers to one minute due to the large crowd signed up for Item 22-0308, Commissioner Nida Allam moved and Commissioner Nimasheena Burns seconded extending speaker time to two minutes, which passed 5-0.

votes.item_title: Acceptance of Draft Community Cat (TNVR) Animal Control Ordinance and Scheduling Public Hearing for June 13 or June 27, 2022 (Item 22-0291)
votes.notes: Later amended at 04:03:56 to set the public hearing for July 11, 2022.
votes.discussion_detail: The Board voted 5-0 to accept the draft TNVR Animal Control Ordinance amendment subject to minor edits or substantive changes in the final draft, schedule a public hearing on June 13 or June 27, 2022 for a final vote, and defer the implementation date to be determined later.

votes.item_title: Motion to Enter Closed Session (GS 143-318.11(a)(5))
votes.discussion_detail: The Board voted unanimously by roll call to enter closed session pursuant to NCGS 143-318.11(a)(5) regarding property acquisition or employment contract negotiation terms.

votes.item_title: Amended Motion to Schedule Community Cat (TNVR) Public Hearing for July 11, 2022 (Item 22-0291)
votes.discussion_detail: After reconvening from closed session, the Board unanimously approved an amendment moving the Community Cat TNVR Animal Control Ordinance public hearing to the July 11, 2022 regular session.

votes.item_title: Approval of Excused Absence for Commissioner Heidi Carter (June 27, 2022 Regular Session)
votes.notes: Commissioner Carter ultimately attended the June 27, 2022 meeting while Vice Chair Jacobs was excused.
votes.discussion_detail: Commissioner Heidi Carter requested an excused absence for the June 27, 2022 regular session (while the Board noted a retroactive excuse for Commissioner Allam's May 19 budget work session was unnecessary); seconded by Commissioner Allam and approved 5-0.

meetings.title: BOCC Budget Work Session #2 - May 19, 2022
meetings.executive_summary: The Board of County Commissioners held its second FY 2022-23 budget work session, reviewing the 10-year $1.8 billion Capital Improvement Plan (CIP), Durham Public Schools (DPS) operating request, and Durham Technical Community College (DTCC) budget. Budget staff presented debt-service projections showing the dedicated 8.61-cent property tax rate held flat in FY 2022-23 alongside a projected 2.5-cent tax increase in FY 2023-24 for a planned November 2022 general obligation bond, while commissioners debated a proposed $500,000 starter allocation for a 1% Public Art Fund. Tension emerged between commissioners and DPS leadership over a remaining $2 million gap between DPS's adjusted $11.875 million essential request and the Manager's $9.875 million recommendation, with commissioners criticizing School Board communication and questioning rising per-pupil spending amid a roughly 1,055-student enrollment drop. DTCC President J.B. Buxton outlined an $789,000 operating increase (+8.81%), expanded Article 46/Durham Promise workforce pathways, the BULLS life-sciences initiative, and bond-funded facility needs, followed by Board follow-up requests on behavioral health returned funds from Alliance Health, Community Paramedicine, CISS, and Soil and Water Conservation. No formal votes were taken during the work session.

agenda_items.title: CIP Financial Overview and 10-Year Capital Financing Plan
agenda_items.discussion_summary: General Manager Claudia Hager and Budget Director Keith Lane reviewed the FY 2022-31 CIP totaling $1.8 billion, including over $900 million for DPS and $106 million for IS&T infrastructure. Staff projected $76 million in FY 2022-23 debt service ($34 million for DPS), $16.9 million in PAYGO projects (including $4.1 million for 500 E. Main affordable housing and detention center window replacements), and holding the dedicated debt-service property tax flat at 8.61 cents with an estimated 2.5-cent increase in FY 2023-24 for a November 2022 GO bond. Commissioners Wendy Jacobs and Nimasheena Burns questioned allocating $500,000 to seed a 1% Public Art program while construction inflation strains capital reserves, and Heidi Carter asked whether $1 million in the $1.5 million Swap Fund could be reallocated.

agenda_items.title: Durham Public Schools (DPS) FY 2022-23 Budget Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Superintendent Dr. Pascal Mubenga, CFO Paul LeSieur, and Budget Director Alex Modesto presented DPS's $12.875 million local funding request—covering $5.3 million in fixed costs, raising minimum teacher supplements from $5,675 to $6,500 plus step increases ($1,135), Lyons Farm Elementary expansion, post-ESSER IT technicians, and $2.6 million in charter school pass-through—compared to the Manager's $9.875 million recommendation ($176 million total, $4,333 per pupil). DPS stated it could absorb ~$1 million for Lyons Farm and IT technicians using lapsed salaries and ESSER funds, narrowing its essential gap to $2 million ($11.875 million total). Commissioners criticized School Board members for failing to communicate directly while mischaracterizing BOCC support publicly, pressed DPS on an ~1,055-student enrollment decline to ~31,300, and discussed classified staff pay ($15.38 moving to $15.78/hour; $17/hour for bus drivers, with universal $17/hour estimated at $4.3-$4.4 million) and ESSER I/II/III spending.

agenda_items.title: Durham Technical Community College (DTCC) FY 2022-23 Budget Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DTCC President J.B. Buxton, CFO Andy Klich, and Chief Academic Officer Dr. Kara Battle presented a $789,000 operating increase (+8.81%) for utilities, facilities, campus security, and a shared apprenticeship coordinator, plus $380,000 in Article 46 Durham Promise growth (to $1.89 million) alongside requests to broaden Article 46 eligibility to non-credit Nurse Aide scholarships, Back to Work overflow, and adult basic skills losses (-$300,000 state FTE drop). Buxton also outlined scaling the BULLS life-sciences youth stipend program via ARPA funds (5 pilot students, 25 across Cohorts 1-2, targeting 60-100 annually plus construction and IT) and major capital plans ($1.1 million CIP HVAC retrofit and 2022 bond funding for Life Sciences, Allied Health, and Bacon/Cooper property acquisition alongside a $1.2 million RTP Bio federal earmark with Wake Tech). Commissioner Nimasheena Burns urged tying corporate economic incentives (JDIG/EDPNC) to private stipend sponsorships, and Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs requested stronger microtransit/GoDurham Connect links to the Northern Durham campus and Treyburn.

agenda_items.title: Commissioner Follow-Up Requests and Behavioral Health Funding Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Commissioners requested follow-up briefings on Community Paramedicine, Community Intervention and Support Services (CISS)—with Burns emphasizing Black and Latino boys and My Brother's Keeper—and Soil and Water Conservation's BETC position and farmer grant staffing. Budget staff confirmed an agenda item for June 2 to amend the Alliance Health contract and return $5 million in unspent behavioral health funds ($2 million to offset county fund balance and $3 million reserved for behavioral health system discussions), while Heidi Carter asked for details on county vehicle replacement policies.

disagreements.issue: DPS Additional $2M Operating Request, Enrollment Decline, and Inter-Board Communication
disagreements.summary: Commissioners challenged DPS leadership over its request for $2-$3 million above the County Manager's $9.875 million increase recommendation amid declining enrollment and frustration with School Board members' public messaging and lack of direct outreach.
disagreements.side_a_position: Question additional ongoing funding above the Manager's $9.875M (+9% per-pupil) recommendation without clearer accountability on declining enrollment (~1,055 drop), classified/certified wage sustainability, and direct School Board communication.
side_a_arguments: Commissioner Nimasheena Burns rebuked School Board members for never contacting commissioners directly while alleging BOCC lacked commitment to DPS teachers and staff.
Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs noted DPS enrollment fell from 32,596 in FY19-20 to ~31,300 projected while county per-pupil funding rose to $4,333.
Chair Brenda A. Howerton stressed fiduciary duty to avoid unnecessary tax hikes amid inflation and warned against shifting narratives when BOCC asks accountability questions.
disagreements.side_b_position: Fund DPS's revised $11.875M essential local operating need (absorbing ~$1M in IT technicians and Lyons Farm expansion internally) to cover fixed costs, teacher salary supplements ($6,500 minimum), and post-pandemic student supports.
side_b_arguments: Superintendent Pascal Mubenga explained pre-pandemic growth reversed by ~1,300 students statewide due to COVID-19 and projected 20,000 more school-age children over five years, noting county dollars fund summer counselors and intensive behavioral COPE staffing (~6-7 adults per 18 students) uncovered by the state.
CFO Paul LeSieur noted charter pass-throughs (+$1.97M/+2.6M) consume substantial local increases and recurring fund balance use is unsustainable.

Commissioner Heidi Carter expressed support for meeting the $11.8M adjusted request while calling for a county-city-DPS community conversation on a sustainable living wage for over 1,000 low-paid school employees.
disagreements.resolution: Vice Chair Jacobs indicated consensus to examine funding DPS's revised $11.8M request while County Manager Kimberly Sowell asked DPS for eight-year enrollment trajectories and charter/fund-balance absorption options before budget adoption.

disagreements.issue: 1% for Public Art Starter Allocation ($500,000) in the Capital Improvement Plan
disagreements.summary: Commissioners questioned whether a proposed $500,000 allocation in the FY 2022-23 CIP to establish a 1% Public Art Fund was an appropriate priority given inflation-driven capital cost overruns.
disagreements.side_a_position: Oppose or scrutinize dedicating $500,000 to a new Public Art program during high inflation and tight debt-service fund balance reserves.
side_a_arguments: Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs expressed surprise at the $500,000 allocation when other urgent needs lack funding and projects like the 300 E. Main parking deck face $4M cost overruns.
Commissioner Nimasheena Burns questioned who requested the allocation and whether commissioners had aligned on spending half a million dollars on public art while human-service needs go unmet.
disagreements.side_b_position: Include the $500,000 starter placeholder based on prior CIP discussions for board review during budget markups.
side_b_arguments: County Manager Kimberly Sowell and GM Claudia Hager explained the line item reflected prior Board policy interest in a 1% art policy for capital projects and could be adjusted through the Ad/Delete budget process.
disagreements.resolution: Staff noted the $500,000 CIP placeholder remained subject to Board removal or modification during upcoming budget work sessions.

meetings.title: BOCC Budget Work Session #1 - May 17, 2022
meetings.executive_summary: The Board of County Commissioners opened its FY 2022-23 budget work sessions with comprehensive briefings on revenue and expenditure drivers, fund balance policies, property tax valuation, and human resources compensation. Budget Director Keith Lane and County Manager Dr. Kimberly Sowell outlined a $794 million total budget ($550 million General Fund, +8.97%) holding the property tax rate flat by pairing $32 million in natural revenue growth—led by property taxes (+$13.9 million) and sales taxes (+$11.5 million total)—with $28 million in General Fund balance, while warning of $30 million in annual structural expenditure pressure going forward. CFO Susan Tezai reviewed the projected $269.6 million FY 2022 General Fund balance and OPEB reserve caps needed to protect Durham County's AAA bond rating, while Tax Administrator Dwane Brinson detailed the delayed 2025 countywide reappraisal, revenue-neutral tax math, and $719 million in exempt property. Human Resources Director Kathy Everett-Perry highlighted an 18% turnover threshold surpassed by +3.9%, 302 upcoming retirement eligibilities, proposed 5.5%–7.5% employee raises (reaching $18.10/hour minimum), free family care at the employee Wellness Clinic, and 4 weeks of Paid Family Leave. No formal votes were taken.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order and FY 2022-23 Budget Revenue and Expenditure Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton called the session to order, and Budget Director Keith Lane, County Manager Kimberly Sowell, and GM Claudia Hager walked through the $794 million recommended budget ($550 million General Fund). Natural revenue growth of $32 million (+$13.9 million GF property tax, +$6.8 million GF sales tax, +$5 million Medicaid Hold Harmless, +$2.7 million Register of Deeds fees, +$3.3 million EMS fees) plus $28 million in appropriated fund balance funds employee COLA/merit raises, +$9.88 million for DPS, +$4.3 million in health insurance, 36.7 new GF FTEs focused on internal support amid a 20% (~400-position) vacancy rate, and vehicle replacements. Commissioners pressed staff for a clearer cumulative tax-rate history chart for taxpayers and asked where an additional $2 million for DPS could be cut without raising taxes.

agenda_items.title: Finance Department Fund Balance Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chief Financial Officer Susan Tezai presented the county's reserve position, projecting $269.6 million in total General Fund balance at FY 2022 year-end ($102.2 million unassigned at FY 2021 close) and explaining how state LGC minimums and county policies (including a 25% cap on OPEB committed reserves) preserve Durham's AAA credit rating. Staff and commissioners discussed revising the fund balance policy to balance rating-agency expectations against capital, inflation, and emergency reserve demands, with Nimasheena Burns underscoring that fund balance should support one-time rather than recurring obligations.

agenda_items.title: Tax Administration Valuation, Reappraisal, and Property Tax Relief Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Tax Administrator Dwane Brinson explained that county properties remain valued at January 1, 2019 assessments until the next countywide reappraisal in 2025, reviewed revenue-neutral calculations showing the 2016 and 2019 tax changes exceeded revenue-neutral, and noted $719 million in exempt property equates to roughly $5.2 million in foregone revenue. Commissioners Wendy Jacobs and Nimasheena Burns voiced deep concern about gentrification and tax-driven displacement in Black and brown neighborhoods ahead of 2025 and urged expanding the county's DSS Low-Income Homeowner Relief program—including reducing its 10-year residency requirement to 5–7.5 years—since state statute caps countywide exemptions.

agenda_items.title: Human Resources Employee Compensation, Retention, and Benefits Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: HR Director Kathy Everett-Perry and benefits staff reported that employee turnover climbed 3.9 percentage points above the 18% county benchmark, with 246 non-retirement separations and 302 staff eligible for retirement in FY 2022-23, alongside 50 vacancies in Public Health and recent mid-year EMS, Youth Home, and Sheriff pay adjustments. Under the recommended budget, 83% of employees (1,529 earning up to $75,000) could receive up to 7.5% combined COLA (3.5%) and merit (up to 4%), lifting the lowest hourly pay from $16.98 to $18.10. New benefits include zero-copay primary care at the Wellness Clinic for employees and dependents, 5 days of funeral leave, pet insurance, and a 4-week Paid Family Leave policy covering serious family illness and COVID quarantine ahead of a broader MAG classification study.

agenda_items.title: Budget Work Session Follow-Up Process and Adjournment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: County Manager Kimberly Sowell and Chair Brenda A. Howerton reviewed the upcoming Ad/Delete list submission process, scheduled follow-up budget questions, and adjourned the work session informally at 03:14:29 without taking formal votes.

disagreements.issue: 2025 Tax Reappraisal Burden, Residential Displacement, and Homeowner Relief Eligibility
disagreements.summary: Commissioners debated how to mitigate rising tax burdens on longtime, lower-income residents ahead of the 2025 reappraisal and 2022/2026 bond referenda within statutory limits.
disagreements.side_a_position: Expand local Low-Income Homeowner Relief access (e.g., shortening the 10-year ownership rule to 5–7.5 years) and transparently present cumulative multi-year tax impacts to protect residents from gentrification and displacement.
side_a_arguments: Commissioner Nimasheena Burns warned rapid gentrification in Black and brown neighborhoods plus stacked tax rate increases (2016, 2019, and upcoming bonds) threatens displacement once 2025 values reset after a six-year gap.
Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs pushed lowering the 10-year residency rule in the county's DSS grant program and tracking multi-year household bill impacts alongside legislative relief advocacy.
disagreements.side_b_position: Statutory uniformity rules prevent Durham County from unilaterally altering property exemptions or deferrals beyond existing state circuit-breaker laws without General Assembly action.
side_b_arguments: Tax Administrator Dwane Brinson noted North Carolina General Statutes strictly govern property exemptions and homestead deferrals ($719M already exempt countywide), requiring grant-based local workarounds or Raleigh legislation.
disagreements.resolution: Staff noted pending DSS Board recommendations to revise the local homeowner grant tenure rule and agreed to provide clearer historical tax-impact graphics for taxpayers.

meetings.title: BOCC - MAY 9th, 2022 Regular Session
meetings.executive_summary: At its May 9, 2022 Regular Session, the Board of County Commissioners heard public comment from DPS Instructional Assistant Association president Sunny Geraldo advocating for higher classified school staff pay before County Manager Dr. Kimberly Sowell formally presented the FY 2022-23 Recommended Budget ($794 million total / $550 million General Fund, holding the tax rate flat). The Board adopted proclamations honoring National EMS Week, Older Americans Month, Children's Mental Health Awareness Month, and National Foster Care Month, and unanimously approved the April 25 minutes (4-0 with Nida Allam absent from the early roll call) and the 15-item Consent Agenda (5-0), highlighted by a renewable energy interlocal agreement with DPS. Commissioners also unanimously adopted formal comments on the Draft FY 2023 Annual Transit Work Program (22-0249) deferring new GoTriangle (0.25 FTE) and City of Durham (3 FTE) staffing requests pending an updated governance ILA and cost-share agreement. Following a unanimous closed session for personnel matters, the Board voted 5-0 to approve a $40,800 consulting contract with Aligned Leadership LLC for Board leadership training.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Announcements, and Public Comment on DPS Classified Pay
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton opened the meeting and Clerk Monica Wallace read announcements covering 500 E. Main construction impacts starting June 6, 2022 primary voting, Durham Pre-K enrollment, and the May 23 budget public hearing. Sunny Geraldo, president of the Durham Public Schools Instructional Assistant Association, urged commissioners to fund the Superintendent's requested classified staff pay increases so custodians, bus drivers, and instructional assistants earn a living wage above $15-$16/hour; Howerton clarified commissioners had not received a prior email requesting a meeting. Commissioners Wendy Jacobs and Nimasheena Burns also highlighted the $1.2 million RTP Bio federal earmark at Durham Tech, Way to Go Durham vanpools/microtransit, and a May 13 health event.

agenda_items.title: Approval of Minutes (April 25, 2022 Regular Session)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Howerton presented the minutes of the April 25, 2022 Regular Session for Board approval with no edits requested. Commissioner Heidi Carter moved approval and the Clerk called the roll, announcing unanimous approval (Burns, Carter, Jacobs, Howerton voting aye; Nida Allam was not recorded on this initial roll call).

agenda_items.title: Ceremonial Proclamations (EMS Week, Older Americans, Children's Mental Health, Foster Care)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The Board issued four May proclamations: National EMS Week (May 15-21, 22-0236) accepted by EMS leaders highlighting behavioral health/crisis integration and retention; Older Americans Month (22-0237) accepted by Durham Center for Senior Life representatives emphasizing senior vaccination, social connection, and caregiver relief; Children's Mental Health Awareness Month (22-0245) read by Wendy Jacobs and accepted by Alliance Health and System of Care staff noting rising youth suicide and crisis demand; and National Foster Care Month (22-0247) read by Nida Allam and accepted by DSS Child Welfare Director Jovetta Whitfield and foster parents.

agenda_items.title: Manager's Recommended FY 2022-23 Budget Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: County Manager Dr. Kimberly Sowell formally presented her recommended $794 million FY 2022-23 budget ($550 million General Fund, +8.97%), maintaining the current property tax rate while funding 5.5%–7.5% employee raises, +$9.88 million for DPS ($176 million total, $4,333 per pupil), +$789,000 for DTCC ($12.1 million operating), 3 additional school health nurses (toward 32 covering 44 schools), 2 maternal health positions, $625,000 in combined food security initiatives, 36 Sheriff vehicles (20 hybrids), 5 Youth Home counselors, ARPA-funded ADA/APD positions, $150,000 for cultural planning, $3.3 million in economic incentives, a renewable energy project manager, and a Mobile Library/Community Outreach unit. Commissioners commended Sowell's inaugural budget presentation ahead of the May 17 and May 19 work sessions and May 23 public hearing.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (15 Items: 22-0209 through 22-0268)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: With no items pulled from the 15-item Consent Agenda, Commissioner Nida Allam moved approval and Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs seconded while highlighting the Durham Public Schools interlocal agreement to join Duke Energy's Green Source Advantage renewable energy program. Passed 5-0 by roll-call vote.

agenda_items.title: 22-0249: Draft FY 2023 Annual Transit Work Program Comments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Transportation Manager Ellen Beckman and Staff Working Group Administrator Aaron Cain presented final recommended BOCC comments on the Draft FY 2023 Durham County Transit Work Program ($3.3 million paratransit facility, $1.8 million Durham Station upgrades, bus-shelter lighting/access). As discussed at the May 4 work session, the comments defer GoTriangle's 0.25 FTE request and the City of Durham's 3 FTE requests pending negotiation of an updated Transit Governance ILA and City-County cost-share policy, call for scope clarity on Fayetteville/Holloway corridor projects, and emphasize prioritizing bus speed, reliability, and BRT building blocks. Moved by Heidi Carter, seconded, and approved 5-0.

agenda_items.title: Closed Session (Personnel) and Aligned Leadership LLC Contract Approval
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The Board voted 5-0 to enter closed session under N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(6) to discuss personnel/board-consulting matters. Upon returning to open session at 02:58:47, Nida Allam moved and Wendy Jacobs seconded hiring Aligned Leadership LLC for $40,800 to facilitate commissioner training and team alignment, passing 5-0 before the Board adjourned by a 5-0 roll-call vote.
